I updated the list of OpenAI API alternatives for LLM Zoomcamp students.

The list includes providers that offer free rate-limited access to their models.

It's needed for the course, but anyone can use it.

Two main categories:

1. Free to use (ongoing free tier, no payment required)

Google Gemini, Groq, Mistral AI, OpenRouter, Cerebras, SambaNova Cloud, GitHub Models, Cloudflare Workers AI, and others.

2. Free signup credits, then paid

Anthropic, xAI Grok, DeepSeek, AWS Bedrock, NVIDIA NIM, and others.

The list was reviewed on June 30, 2026. Free tiers change often, so double-check current limits before relying on them.

Full list: https://github.com/DataTalksClub/llm-zoomcamp/blob/main/awesome-llms.md#openai-api-alternatives

posts.text:
In one week, we have a workshop on tracking and personalizing AI agents with Snowplow and the Vercel AI SDK.

Your agent can see the chat history but not what the user is doing in the product. If you want the agent to respond based on the user's current session, you need to capture that context and make it available to the model.

This workshop shows how to do that with a Next.js travel chatbot.

The approach:

1. Track client behavior (page views, clicks, filters)
2. Track server-side events (purchases, bookings)
3. Track agent decisions (tool calls, outcomes)
4. Validate events against schemas in real time
5. Compute session attributes with Snowplow Signals
6. Inject those attributes into the system prompt

You'll set up the pipeline, add tracking at each layer, and use live session data to shape the agent's responses.

payload.preview:
Sometimes I want an agent to experiment with AWS while I'm away from my laptop.

I don't want admin...

posts.text:
Sometimes I want an agent to experiment with AWS while I'm away from my laptop.

I don't want admin AWS credentials on my phone.

I don't want to SSH into my laptop from somewhere outside.

And I don't want an agent hitting AWS whenever it wants, especially if it can provision expensive resources.

So I reused the credential endpoint I built for workshops.

The remote sandbox points its AWS credential URI at a Lambda. Then I built a small phone app that toggles that Lambda on and off.

When the toggle is on, the Lambda returns temporary credentials.

When it is off, the sandbox asks for credentials and fails.

The access can be limited to a short window, for example 15 minutes or an hour. I can turn it on from my phone, let the agent run an experiment in the sandbox, and turn it off again.

This is the third use case for the same mechanism:

- Workshops with 50 or 60 people
- Coding agents in a sandbox AWS account
- Phone-controlled temporary AWS access

I wrote the full story in my latest newsletter:

https://alexeyondata.substack.com/p/the-system-i-built-for-aws-access

I learned this the expensive way after one...

posts.text:
A coding agent should never have a path to production.

I learned this the expensive way after one of my agents dropped a production database. That incident changed how I think about cloud access for agents.

Now my setup is different.

Agents run on a remote sandbox server. The server is disposable. If an agent breaks it, I can recreate it.

Real deployments go through CI/CD. Agents can write Terraform and push changes to GitHub, but I apply production infrastructure changes myself.

When an agent needs to experiment with AWS, it gets access only to a separate sandbox account.

That access is:

- Temporary
- Scoped
- Revocable
- Not connected to production

I wrote about the full system in my latest newsletter: https://alexeyondata.substack.com/p/the-system-i-built-for-aws-access

posts.text:
I needed to grant 50-60 workshop participants access to AWS.

They had to provision resources from their own machines. I didn't want them to install anything. I didn't want to copy AWS keys into a repo, an email, a chat, or a slide.

And I definitely didn't want them anywhere near my main AWS account.

So I built a credential endpoint.

The short version:

- A Lambda assumes an AWS role
- The AWS SDK fetches temporary credentials from a URL
- The environment points to that URL with `AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI`
- The workshop runs from GitHub Codespaces
- Participants get access without ever seeing a long-lived key

What started as a workshop setup later became useful for coding agents too.

I don't want agents to have permanent access to AWS. I want them in a sandbox account, with temporary credentials, and with a way to turn access off.

I wrote about the full system in my latest newsletter: https://alexeyondata.substack.com/p/the-system-i-built-for-aws-access

posts.text:
With function calling, the LLM does not run your Python function.

What happens is a protocol:

1. You describe the tool
2. The model decides to use it
3. The model returns a structured tool call
4. Your code parses the arguments
5. Your code runs the function
6. Your code sends the result back to the model
7. The model uses the result to answer

The model can choose:

- Which tool name to call
- Which arguments to pass
- Whether another tool call is needed

But your application is still responsible for executing the function and deciding what to trust.

In my workshop on going from RAG to agents, I showed how tool calling provides the model with a structured way to request actions.

But it's important to remember that it does not remove the need for application logic, validation, logging, retries, or guardrails.

Recording: https://youtube.com/live/RAqLWJsLZb4

Want to learn how to build RAG and agents? Join LLM Zoomcamp, our free course that starts on June 8: https://github.com/DataTalksClub/llm-zoomcamp

posts.text:
Most agent frameworks are wrapping the same basic loop:

Call the model.
If the response contains tool calls, execute them.
Append the tool results to the message history.
Call the model again.
Repeat until the response has no tool calls.

Frameworks add useful things around this:

- Tool registration
- Schema generation
- Message history handling
- Callback hooks
- Debug views
- Cost tracking
- Error handling

But the core loop is still small enough to understand.

In my workshop about going from RAG to agents, we implemented it manually first:

- Start with instructions and a user question
- Send them to the model
- Check every response item
- If it is a function call, run the function
- Add both the tool call and output to the history
- Stop when there are no function calls left

Once you understand this, agent frameworks become easier to evaluate.

The framework matters. The mental model matters more.

Recording: https://youtube.com/live/RAqLWJsLZb4

posts.text:
API costs add up fast when you make many model calls.

This is especially true for evaluations.

When evaluating many prompts, model versions, datasets, or agent traces, you often do not need the results immediately. In these cases, latency can become something you trade for lower cost.

On June 22, we'll have a 2-hour AI Shipping Labs workshop on this: Saving Money on API Calls with Batch and Flex Processing

We'll look at:

- When evals can run asynchronously instead of inline
- How to use OpenAI Batch API for eval runs and delayed jobs
- How Flex processing helps with lower-priority Responses / Chat Completions calls
- Prompt caching, model choice, and request shaping as cost levers
- How to structure an eval pipeline so slower, cheaper calls are acceptable
- Failure modes: timeouts, retries, expired batches, and when not to delay

Bring an existing eval idea or a workflow with repeated API calls if you want to reason through it live.

Available for AI Shipping Labs community members with Main plan and higher.

posts.text:
Most agents break the first time they hit production.

Not because the logic is wrong, but because the infrastructure isn't ready for failures, restarts, and long-running workflows.

Nicholas Lotz will cover the execution layer that makes agents durable in production.

We rescheduled this workshop to August 17.

If you've built an agent that works in a notebook but haven't deployed it yet, you're probably about to hit the same set of questions.

What happens when the process restarts mid-execution?

How do you retry a tool call that timed out without duplicating side effects?

How do you pause for human approval when the approval might take two days?

How do you trace which step failed and why?

Nicholas will cover the infrastructure patterns you need:

- State persistence outside the agent process
- Recovery after crashes and deployments
- Retry logic with execution history
- Human-in-the-loop workflows that can wait
- Tracing and observability for multi-step workflows

By the end, you'll know when you need durable execution and how to structure the layer around your agent loop.

4:30 PM - 6:00 PM CEST
YouTube

posts.text:
Retrieval settings often start as gut feeling.

In the workshop, I had one too.

For FAQ search, I assumed the `question` field should be boosted more than the `answer` field.

The reasoning sounded plausible:

If the user asks a question, matching the FAQ question should matter more than matching random words in the answer.

Then we evaluated it.

We generated a ground-truth set, ran search for each question, computed hit rate and MRR, and tried different boost values.

The result did not fully match my initial assumption.

Boosting the question field too much made the ranking worse. The better settings gave more relative weight to the answer text and less to the section field.

This is why evaluation is useful.

It turns retrieval tuning from opinion into an experiment.

You can compare:

- Field boost values
- Top K values
- Text search vs vector search
- Hybrid search variants
- Different embedding models
- Rerankers

For small datasets, grid search is enough.

For expensive evaluations, use smarter optimization.

The important part is not the specific boost value. The important part is having a repeatable way to check whether a retrieval change improved the metric that matters.

Watch my latest workshop on evaluating RAG and agents to learn how to do it: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WUGtDveIe7A

Or join LLM Zoomcamp, our free course about building LLM-based applications: https://github.com/DataTalksClub/llm-zoomcamp

posts.text:
Hit rate and MRR answer two different retrieval questions.

Hit rate asks:

"Did the expected document appear anywhere in the top results?"

If the right document is in the top 5, it counts as a hit.

This is useful, but it ignores position.

The expected document in position 1 and position 5 both count the same.

MRR, mean reciprocal rank, adds position.

If the expected document is:

- Rank 1: score 1.0
- Rank 2: score 0.5
- Rank 3: score 0.33
- Rank 4: score 0.25
- Not found: score 0

Then we average this across all evaluation questions.

For RAG, this matters because top context is usually more useful than buried context.

An LLM may still recover the answer if the right chunk is third or fifth, especially when top K is small.

But higher-ranked relevant context is easier to use, cheaper to inspect, and less likely to be diluted by irrelevant text.

So I usually look at both:

- Hit rate: are we finding the answer?
- MRR: are we ranking it well?

The first tells you coverage.

The second tells you retrieval quality.

Watch my latest workshop on evaluating RAG and agents to learn how to do it: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WUGtDveIe7A

Or join LLM Zoomcamp, our free course about building LLM-based applications: https://github.com/DataTalksClub/llm-zoomcamp

posts.text:
A small detail makes RAG evaluation much easier:

Give every source record a stable ID.

When you generate evaluation questions, keep the ID of the record that produced the question.

Then retrieval evaluation becomes straightforward:

1. Run search with the generated question
2. Get the top K documents
3. Compare their IDs with the expected ID

Without IDs, you end up comparing text.

That gets messy quickly:

- Answers may be paraphrased
- Similar FAQ records may overlap
- Formatting may change
- Duplicates may appear
- Document chunks may be regenerated

IDs give you a clean join key between:

- The original knowledge base
- The generated ground-truth questions
- The retrieved search results
- The evaluation records

In the workshop, I also used structured outputs when generating questions.

That matters for automation.

If the LLM returns a predictable object, you can store it, validate it, and run metrics without manually cleaning text every time.

For RAG evals, stable IDs plus structured outputs are not fancy. They are plumbing.

But good plumbing is what lets you measure reliably.

Watch my latest workshop on evaluating RAG and agents to learn how to do it: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WUGtDveIe7A

Or join LLM Zoomcamp, our free course about building LLM-based applications: https://github.com/DataTalksClub/llm-zoomcamp

posts.text:
When you build a new RAG assistant, you often do not have real user logs yet.

But you still need an evaluation set.

One practical starting point is synthetic data.

Take a known FAQ record:

- Question
- Answer
- Document ID

Then ask an LLM to generate several realistic user questions that could lead to that answer.

Now you have pairs like:

- Generated user question
- Expected document ID

This is enough to start evaluating retrieval.

For each generated question, run search and check whether the expected document appears in the top results.

This gives you a first version of:

- Hit rate
- MRR
- Failed query examples
- Retrieval parameter comparisons

There is an important caveat.

Synthetic questions are usually too clean. They may resemble the FAQ text more than real user behavior.

So I treat them as a bootstrap, not as the final evaluation.

The next step is collecting real user questions, labeling them, and adjusting the synthetic generator so it better matches production data.

But synthetic evals are still much better than changing retrieval settings by gut feeling.

Watch my latest workshop on evaluating RAG and agents to learn how to do it: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WUGtDveIe7A

Or join LLM Zoomcamp, our free course about building LLM-based applications: https://github.com/DataTalksClub/llm-zoomcamp

posts.text:
Exact string matching is usually the wrong way to evaluate RAG answers.

The generated answer can use different words and still be correct.

That is why LLM-as-judge is useful.

Give the judge:

- The user question
- The reference answer
- The answer generated by the RAG system

Ask whether the generated answer is semantically equivalent to the reference answer.

In the workshop, I used structured output with:

- A verdict: good or bad
- Reasoning: why the judge made that decision

The reasoning is not mainly for the user. It is for debugging and calibration.

If the judge marks a bad answer as good, the evaluation score becomes misleading.

So the judge needs its own evaluation loop:

1. Sample judged examples
2. Manually inspect them
3. Check whether the judge is too strict or too lenient
4. Adjust the prompt
5. Rerun and compare

Automated judging is useful.

But it is not a replacement for human judgment. It is a way to scale evaluation after you have checked that the judge behaves reasonably.

Watch my latest workshop on evaluating RAG and agents to learn how to do it: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WUGtDveIe7A

posts.text:
For a plain RAG pipeline, we can evaluate the final answer against a reference answer.

For agents, that is not enough.

An agent can reach a decent final answer through a bad path.

For example:

- It calls search too many times
- It rewrites the query in a harmful way
- It ignores a useful tool result
- It uses the wrong tool first
- It spends unnecessary tokens and latency

So agent evaluation should include the trajectory.

The trajectory is the sequence of actions the agent took:

- Tool calls
- Tool arguments
- Tool outputs
- Intermediate decisions
- Final answer

Then the judge can evaluate two things:

1. Was the final answer correct?
2. Was the tool-use path reasonable?

This matters because production failures are not only wrong answers.

They are also slow answers, expensive answers, unstable loops, unnecessary retries, and actions that should not have happened.

For agentic RAG, I would store the trajectory by default.

If you cannot inspect the path, you cannot reliably debug the agent.

Watch my latest workshop on evaluating RAG and agents to learn how to do it: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WUGtDveIe7A

posts.text:
A RAG system has several places where things can fail.

The answer can be bad because the model generated poorly. But often the answer is bad earlier than that: retrieval didn't find the right context.

That is why I like evaluating search separately before evaluating the full RAG pipeline.

For a basic RAG assistant, the flow is:

1. User asks a question
2. Search retrieves candidate documents
3. The prompt includes those documents
4. The LLM generates an answer

If step 2 is weak, the rest of the pipeline is already in trouble.

posts.text:
With function calling, the LLM does not run your Python function.

What happens is a protocol:

1. You describe the tool
2. The model decides to use it
3. The model returns a structured tool call
4. Your code parses the arguments
5. Your code runs the function
6. Your code sends the result back to the model
7. The model uses the result to answer

The model can choose:

- Which tool name to call
- Which arguments to pass
- Whether another tool call is needed

But your application is still responsible for executing the function and deciding what to trust.

In my workshop on going from RAG to agents, I showed how tool calling provides the model with a structured way to request actions.

But it's important to remember that it does not remove the need for application logic, validation, logging, retries, or guardrails.

Recording: https://youtube.com/live/RAqLWJsLZb4

posts.text:
Your first RAG implementation should be easy to replace.

In my recent workshop, we started with a modular setup:

1. Search
2. Build prompt
3. Call LLM

Then we moved the logic into reusable components.

It's important because the first version is rarely the final version.

You may start with:

- MinSearch and later move to SQLite search, Elasticsearch, Postgres, or vector search.
- OpenAI and later try Anthropic, Gemini, or a local model.
- A notebook and later move the logic into a service.

If everything is mixed together, every change becomes painful.

A better pattern is to keep dependencies explicit: the search index, the LLM client, the prompt template, the course filter, and the model name.

Then replacing one part does not require rewriting the whole assistant.

Check out my workshop recording to build your first RAG application: https://www.youtube.com/live/KSItlTAsMsk?si=xQDsAgtnzB9wAC4-

posts.text:
Hard truth: You don't always need an agent.

Sometimes you need parsing, retrieval, or a deterministic workflow with a few LLM calls.

An agent becomes useful when the system needs to decide what action to take next: which tool to call, with which arguments, in which order, and whether another attempt is needed.

But that flexibility is not free.

When you add an agent, you usually introduce more model calls, latency, traces to inspect, failure modes, and opportunities for the system to behave unexpectedly.

My default approach is:

1. Start with the simplest workflow
2. Measure where it fails
3. Add tools where the model needs external information or actions
4. Add an agentic loop only when fixed control flow is too rigid
5. Monitor cost, traces, and failure modes from the start

Watch this workshop recording to learn more about my approach: https://youtube.com/live/RAqLWJsLZb4

posts.text:
Most agent frameworks are wrapping the same basic loop:

Call the model.
If the response contains tool calls, execute them.
Append the tool results to the message history.
Call the model again.
Repeat until the response has no tool calls.

Frameworks add useful things around this:

- Tool registration
- Schema generation
- Message history handling
- Callback hooks
- Debug views
- Cost tracking
- Error handling

But the core loop is still small enough to understand.

In my workshop about going from RAG to agents, we implemented it manually first:

- Start with instructions and a user question
- Send them to the model
- Check every response item
- If it is a function call, run the function
- Add both the tool call and output to the history
- Stop when there are no function calls left

Once you understand this, agent frameworks become easier to evaluate.

The framework matters. The mental model matters more.

Recording: https://youtube.com/live/RAqLWJsLZb4

posts.text:
When people talk about "agent memory", it can sound abstract.

In the simplest useful agent, memory is just the message history.

For a tool-using agent, that history usually includes:

- The developer instructions
- The user message
- The model's tool call
- The tool output
- The next model message
- Any follow-up user messages

This is why traces are so useful.

If the final answer is wrong, you can inspect and debug the chain:

Did the model choose the right tool?
Did it pass the right arguments?
Did the tool return the expected result?
Was the result added back to the conversation correctly?

Most agent bugs become much easier to understand once you treat memory as explicit state, not as something mysterious inside the model.

Recording: https://youtube.com/live/RAqLWJsLZb4

posts.text:
Next DataTalksClub workshop:

Running Durable Agents in Production

With Nicholas Lotz
Tuesday, June 16
4:30 PM - 6:00 PM CET
YouTube

If you have already built a basic agent loop, you probably saw the next set of questions quickly.

Where do you store state?

How do you recover after a failed tool call?

How do you wait for human approval?

How do you debug the exact step that failed?

This workshop is about the code and infrastructure around the loop.

We will cover:

- Why in-process agent loops fail in production
- How to persist workflow state outside the agent process
- How to resume after process death, deploys, and failures
- How to retry tool calls without losing execution history or duplicating side effects
- How to add human approval steps that write pending state and resume later
- How to inspect traces for LLM calls, tool calls, timing, token usage, errors, and retry attempts
- How durable execution fits with RAG, evaluation, monitoring, and production AI systems

By the end, you should have a clearer mental model for the execution layer you need around the agent loop.

Register here: https://luma.com/wz20rm8n

But that flexibility is not free.

When you add an agent, you usually introduce more model calls, latency, traces to inspect, failure modes, and opportunities for the system to behave unexpectedly.

My default approach is:

1. Start with the simplest workflow
2. Measure where it fails
3. Add tools where the model needs external information or actions
4. Add an agentic loop only when fixed control flow is too rigid
5. Monitor cost, traces, and failure modes from the start

posts.text:
A plain RAG system usually follows a fixed path:

1. Take the user question
2. Search the knowledge base
3. Put the results into a prompt
4. Ask the LLM to answer

This works well when the query is clean and the retrieval step finds the right context.

It gets weaker when the query is messy.

In the workshop, I used a small example: a student asks how to run Ollama locally, but types it in a way that lexical search does not match well. In a fixed RAG flow, we already committed to the search query before the LLM sees the results.

With agentic RAG, the flow changes.

Instead of forcing search first, we tell the LLM:

"Here is the user's question. Here is a search tool you can use."

Then the LLM can decide:

- Whether search is needed
- What query to send
- Whether to rewrite the query
- Whether another search is needed

This is the important shift.

Agentic RAG is not magic. It is still retrieval plus generation. But the retrieval step becomes something the model can control through tool calls.

That makes the system more flexible, especially when the user's input is incomplete, misspelled, or phrased differently from the documents.

It also makes the system more complex. Now you have more calls, more state, and more things to observe.

So I would not start every RAG project with an agent. I would start with the fixed flow, measure where it fails, and add agentic behavior only where the system needs that extra flexibility.

Recording: https://youtube.com/live/RAqLWJsLZb4

posts.text:
When your agent fails, you need to answer specific questions:

- Which step was running?
- Which tool was called?
- What arguments did we send to the tool?
- What did the tool return?
- Was this a timeout, a bad input, a rate limit, or an LLM decision?
- How long did each step take?
- How much did it cost?
- Can we retry safely?
- Can we resume from the failed step?

Without traces and per-step history, you are mostly reading logs and guessing.

For an agent workflow, I would want to see the run ID, step ID, prompt version, model response, tool name, tool arguments, tool response, latency, token usage, error, and retry count.

posts.text:
Adding a human approval step to an agent looks small in code.

Usually it looks like this:

1. The agent prepares an action.
2. A person reviews it.
3. The agent continues.

But now you have a workflow that may need to wait.

What happens if approval takes two hours or two days?

What happens if the worker process restarts?

What happens if the deployment finishes while the workflow is waiting?

What happens if the approver rejects the step and the agent needs to compensate or choose a different path?

On June 16, Nicholas Lotz will join @DataTalksClub to cover human-in-the-loop workflows, retries, timeouts, traces, failure recovery, and deployment patterns for agents that need to run outside a demo.

posts.text:
Setting up tool calling for your agent is a big step.

But it does not mean the agent is ready for production.

It means the agent can call a function with a schema.

Once you put it in a real workflow, you need to answer smaller questions:

- Where is the state stored?
- Do you save the tool input and output for each step?
- What happens if the tool call times out?
- Can you retry without creating a duplicate ticket, payment, message, or database write?
- Can the workflow wait for approval and continue tomorrow?
- Can you resume after a deploy?

This is what we will cover in the DataTalksClub workshop "Running Durable Agents in Production" with Nicholas Lotz.

We will focus on the pieces around the agent loop that are easy to miss at first:

- Server-side state instead of process-local memory
- Per-step execution history
- Retry policies, timeouts, and idempotency for tool calls
- Timeouts and recovery paths
- Human approval steps that can wait without keeping a worker alive
- Traces for debugging prompts, model calls, tool calls, timing, token usage, and failures

The useful outcome is practical: you can explain what ran, what failed, what was retried, and where the workflow should continue.

posts.text:
Most of my coding now happens on my phone.

The work doesn't stop, so most of my coding happens on trains, buses, between school runs, and on planes.

- tmuxctl to make tmux usable from a phone
- Voice input through Typeless (I stopped typing prompts months ago)
- A custom Android app to auto-forward remote ports (Claude Code built it)
- Throwaway HTML tools when I need visual work

Read more about it in my latest post: https://alexeyondata.substack.com/p/the-system-i-built-to-ship-code-from

posts.text:
Don't start a RAG project with vector search by default.

Start with a text search.

It is simpler:

- No embedding model
- No vector database
- No extra query-time encoding step
- Fewer dependencies
- Easier debugging

Vector search is useful when users ask the same thing with different words.

For example:

"Can I still join the course?" or "Can I still enroll in the program?"

These are semantically close, but a lexical search may miss the connection if the words don't overlap.

That's where embeddings help, but they also add overhead.

You need to encode the dataset, store the vectors, encode each query, choose a search backend, and evaluate whether the improvement is worth it.

My rule:

1. Build version 1 with text search
2. Then evaluate
- If vector search gives a meaningful improvement, add it.
- If the improvement is marginal, the complexity may not be worth it.

-> Use my workshop recording to learn how vector search fits into RAG: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BC3NsRUNEIg&t=714s

- Collect traces from an LLM pipeline
- Instrument LLM calls and retrieval steps
- Store chat history and user interactions
- Collect user feedback on generated answers
- Track answer quality over time
- Use dashboards to inspect system behavior
- Run evaluations on production traces

Before deployment, we evaluate on test data. After deployment, we use traces, feedback, and production metrics to understand what actually happens in the system. This helps us detect issues in retrieval, generation, latency, cost, and answer quality.

posts.text:
Vector search adds a second lifecycle to your RAG application.

With text search, indexing is almost instant for small datasets.

With vector search, you need to generate embeddings for every document. That takes time.

You don't want this to happen every time the application starts.

A better structure:

1. Ingestion process

Load documents, generate embeddings, store them in a database.

2. Application process

Load the existing index and answer user queries.

This is why persistence matters.

For a demo, everything can live in one notebook. But for an application, ingestion and serving should be separate.

Check out my workshop recording to learn how vector search fits into RAG: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BC3NsRUNEIg&t=714s

Why retrieve top 5 documents instead of only top 1 in RAG?

Because the answer isn't always in one...

posts.text:
Why retrieve top 5 documents instead of only top 1 in RAG?

Because the answer isn't always in one document.

Sometimes:

- One document has the direct answer
- Another adds an important condition
- The top result is close but not sufficient
- The second or third result is actually more useful

Then the LLM can use the retrieved context to produce a better answer

Top 5 is not a magic number; you can choose this number based on your dataset.

You choose it and evaluate the results to make a final decision:

- Maybe top 3 is enough.
- Maybe top 10 improves recall.
- Maybe too many documents add noise.

The important part here is to treat retrieval as something you measure and evaluate.

posts.text:
A basic RAG application is just three steps.

1. Search: Find documents that are likely to contain the answer.

2. Build prompt: Turn the user question and search results into context the model can use.

3. Call the LLM: Generate the final answer.

That’s enough for the first version.

In my recent workshop, we built this with a course FAQ assistant. A student asks a question, search returns relevant FAQ entries, we build a prompt with the question and context, and the LLM answers.

The useful part of this structure is that every step is visible.

You can inspect search results.
You can print the prompt.
You can change the model.
You can improve retrieval without touching the LLM call.

Before adding frameworks, agents, or orchestration, make sure these three functions work.

A simple RAG pipeline is much easier to debug when you can see each step.

Check out my workshop recording to build your first RAG application: https://www.youtube.com/live/KSItlTAsMsk?si=xQDsAgtnzB9wAC4-

posts.text:
Your first RAG implementation should be easy to replace.

In my recent workshop, we started with a modular setup:

1. Search
2. Build prompt
3. Call LLM

Then we moved the logic into reusable components.

It's important because the first version is rarely the final version.

You may start with:

- MinSearch and later move to SQLite search, Elasticsearch, Postgres, or vector search.
- OpenAI and later try Anthropic, Gemini, or a local model.
- A notebook and later move the logic into a service.

If everything is mixed together, every change becomes painful.

A better pattern is to keep dependencies explicit: the search index, the LLM client, the prompt template, the course filter, and the model name.

Then replacing one part does not require rewriting the whole assistant.

Check out my workshop recording to build your first RAG application: https://www.youtube.com/live/KSItlTAsMsk?si=xQDsAgtnzB9wAC4-

posts.text:
Don't start a RAG project with vector search by default.

Start with a text search.

It is simpler:

- No embedding model
- No vector database
- No extra query-time encoding step
- Fewer dependencies
- Easier debugging

Vector search is useful when users ask the same thing with different words.

For example:

"Can I still join the course?" or "Can I still enroll in the program?"

These are semantically close, but a lexical search may miss the connection if the words don't overlap.

That's where embeddings help, but they also add overhead.

You need to encode the dataset, store the vectors, encode each query, choose a search backend, and evaluate whether the improvement is worth it.

My rule:

1. Build version 1 with text search
2. Then evaluate
- If vector search gives a meaningful improvement, add it.
- If the improvement is marginal, the complexity may not be worth it.

-> Use my workshop recording to learn how vector search fits into RAG: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BC3NsRUNEIg&t=714s

posts.text:
Most AI engineers should learn RAG before fine-tuning.

Both approaches can help with domain-specific knowledge, but they work differently.

With fine-tuning, you change the model weights.

With RAG, you keep the model as a black box and give it relevant context at request time.

For many applications, RAG is the more practical first step.

1. It is easier to update. If your knowledge base changes, you update the documents or the index. You don’t retrain the model.

2. It works with different LLM providers. The knowledge layer is separate from the model.

3. It is also easier to debug. You can inspect retrieved documents, prompts, answers, and failure modes.

Fine-tuning has valid use cases, but it requires more infrastructure, more specialized tooling, and more careful evaluation.

My default recommendation: start with RAG.

Use fine-tuning only when you have a clear reason that retrieval and prompting cannot solve.

posts.text:
RAG demos often look simple because the data is already clean.

In my recent workshop, I used FAQ data from DataTalksClub courses. The data was already available via a JSON endpoint, so we could load, index, and search it.

In real projects, this part is usually not smooth.

You may need to:

- Parse documents
- Scrape pages
- Clean HTML
- Normalize fields
- Remove duplicates
- Add metadata
- Decide what should be searchable and filterable

If the data is messy, the LLM can still produce fluent answers. But the answers may be incomplete, outdated, or wrong.

For many RAG systems, improving the data preparation step gives more value than changing the prompt.

posts.text:
A plain LLM can give a helpful answer and still be wrong for your application.

In the workshop, we used a simple student question:

"I just discovered the course. Can I still join?"

When we sent it directly to the LLM, it gave a generic answer: if enrollment is still open, you can usually join.

That sounds reasonable, but it doesn't know our actual course policy.

Then we added the FAQ context and sent the question along with it.

The answer became specific: yes, you can join, but if you want a certificate, you need to submit your project while submissions are open.

That's the basic idea of RAG.

- The model handles generation.
- Search handles access to your knowledge base.
- The prompt connects the user's question with the retrieved context.

posts.text:
If you've written a Claude Code skill or tuned a system prompt, you probably want to know if the change actually helped.

Ernest from JetBrains walked through this evaluation question in a recent workshop.

His example: a skill JetBrains built to help AI analyze failing builds on TeamCity. The question was whether the skill helps the AI give better answers about build failures.

Here's the shape of his eval:

1. Arrange. Start with a case where you know the right answer. In Ernest's example, a failing build was caused by a null pointer exception. Point the AI at a real server, or mock the API responses it would query.

2. Act. Ask the question the skill is meant to help with: "Why did this build fail?"

3. Assert. Check that the answer contains "null pointer exception." Optionally, check it doesn't drift into things you've seen the AI hallucinate about.

Run this evaluation twice:
1. Once with your skill loaded
2. Once without it.

The difference is what your skill is worth.

- Good in both cases? Your skill might not be doing much.
- Good with, bad without? Evidence that the skill is pulling its weight.
- Bad in both? Different problem.

The first version can be ten cases in a spreadsheet. No infrastructure, no agent. Just scenarios with known-good answers, a way to grade the output (a substring check is often enough), and the discipline to run each case more than once.

If you want to see how JetBrains scales this across hundreds of tasks in parallel, and how SWE-bench works under the hood, watch the full workshop: https://www.youtube.com/live/_FUj6gSHbCU

Ernest from...

posts.text:
If you've written unit tests, you already understand how AI agents get evaluated.

Ernest from JetBrains walked through SWE-bench in one of our recent workshops and shared this framing:

1. Arrange: Check out a real open-source repo at the exact commit before a bug was fixed. Drop in the GitHub issue text as the prompt.

2. Act: Let the AI agent do its thing: read the code, propose a patch, apply it.

3. Assert: Run the tests the human maintainer wrote in the PR that actually fixed the bug. Did the agent's patch make them pass? Did it break anything that used to work?

Same three steps you'd use for any unit test. The difference is what happens when you run it twice.

A unit test is deterministic. Same input, same output. If it passes today and fails tomorrow with no code change, you've found a flaky test and you fix it.

AI evaluation isn't like that. The model is stochastic by design, so the same prompt can get slightly different answers every time. A single failed run tells you almost nothing.

Ernest's example from the session: a 30-task eval that usually hits ~70% came back at 10% once. Nothing had changed.

The rule he gave: one failure is noise. Three failures in a row are a signal.

If you're starting to build evals for an agent, a skill, or even a prompt, watch the full session to learn more about agent evaluation: https://www.youtube.com/live/_FUj6gSHbCU

posts.text:
If you've seen a coding model release lately, chances are it was scored on SWE-bench. The number usually makes it into the announcement.

But what does the benchmark actually measure?

I sat down with Ernest from JetBrains to find out.

SWE-bench (the standard one, not the multilingual variant) is entirely Python.

We pulled up the dataset live during the session. Every repo in it: Django, Astropy, scikit-learn, SymPy, Sphinx, pylint, pvlib, and a handful of others.

12 Python repositories in total. The "multilingual" version is a separate, smaller dataset.

So when a model claims a SWE-bench score, what's actually being measured is:

Can it resolve real GitHub issues in 12 Python codebases, judged against the same tests the human maintainer wrote in the PR that fixed the bug?

These are mature projects with non-trivial issues, so the benchmark isn't trivial to beat.

But a high score doesn't mean a model is "X% good at software engineering". What would be more accurate to say is that a model is "X% good at Python bugs in a slice of the ecosystem."

In the workshop, Ernest also walked through how models have started recognizing specific issues from the benchmark, which is its own problem.

If you've been experimenting with agent evaluation, the full session is worth an hour.

We went through:

- How the benchmark is structured
- Why one failed eval run is noise and three is signal
- How JetBrains runs 300 evaluations in parallel without bankrupting themselves on tokens
- How to build your own eval without building an agent

Watch it here: https://www.youtube.com/live/_FUj6gSHbCU

posts.text:
I built a system that generates children's books for my son with AI.

He has very specific interests. He asks for books about narrow topics like metals, signal sirens, and other things that are hard to find as children's books.

So I started experimenting.

First, I used ChatGPT to create a book about metals: palladium, tin, magnesium, titanium, beryllium, lithium, tungsten, and a few others.

Then I tried coding agents to generate more books.

Eventually, I built a dedicated book generator.

In my recent newsletter, I explain:

- How the first book about metals started the project
- Why direct ChatGPT generation was not enough
- How coding agents helped create the first versions
- Why I later built a dedicated book generator
- How the current pipeline plans, writes, formats, and packages books
- How audio, EPUB, and Amazon KDP outputs are generated
- What happened when I tried to publish one of the books on Amazon

It's a practical example of using AI for a real, narrow, personal use case.

Read the full newsletter here: https://alexeyondata.substack.com/p/building-an-ai-book-generator-with
By the way, the code is open-source: https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/ai-book-generator

posts.text:
I was in Darmstadt for @PyConDE, the Python and PyData conference.

I did a series of interviews with people from the Python, PyData, AI, tooling, developer advocacy, and community organizing worlds.

At PyConDE 2026, we talked about how Python is evolving in the age of AI, why conferences still matter, and how technical communities are sustained by people who teach, organize, mentor, build tools, and create spaces for others to grow.

I spoke with:

🔸 Jessica Greene from Ecosia and PyLadies Berlin about machine learning engineering, community spaces, career support, and AI as an amplification tool.

🔸 Cheuk Ting Ho from JetBrains about PyCharm, developer advocacy, free-threaded Python, and technical storytelling.

🔸 Sebastian Raschka about AI education, “from scratch” explanations, LLMs, reasoning models, and why fundamentals still matter.

🔸 Kyle Into from Meta about Pyrefly, Python type checking, large codebases, and how better type information helps both developers and AI coding agents.

🔸 Valerio Maggio about developer advocacy, PyConDE lightning talks, PyCon Italia, volunteering, and sustainable community organizing.

🔸 Tereza Iofciu about Data Diplomat, career uncertainty, leadership, and how data professionals can navigate changing expectations.

🔸 Irina Saribekova about Python conference organizing, PyData Berlin, PyConDE, and helping technical people share knowledge through talks, articles, meetups, podcasts, and conferences.

A common theme across these conversations:

AI is changing the tools and workflows, but fundamentals, mentorship, communication, and technical communities still matter.

Thank you Jessica Greene, Cheuk Ting Ho, Sebastian Raschka, Kyle Into, Valerio Maggio, Tereza Iofciu, and Irina Saribekova for sharing your time and thoughts.

Listed to the interviews here: https://creators.spotify.com/pod/profile/datatalksclub/episodes/PyConDE-2026-Conference-Interviews-e3id9if/a-ack4apu

Last week, I ran the first workshop inside AI Shipping Labs: "Deploy Your AI Agent Project to Production with FastAPI and a Vector DB"

During the session, we:

- took an existing Telegram bot agent
- built a frontend for it
- packaged it as a Docker image
- deployed it on Render

The format was more freestyle than usual.

I prepared some parts in advance, but a lot of the session was improvised. I wanted it to feel closer to real project work, where you don’t just follow slides, but deal with the actual steps, decisions, and small issues that come up while shipping.

It ran for about two hours, longer than planned, but the feedback was good.

Based on this, I want to do more sessions like this inside AI Shipping Labs: practical, project-based, and close to how real development work happens.

The recording and code are already available in the AI Shipping Labs Slack community.

posts.text:
SWE-bench is one of the better-known benchmarks for evaluating AI coding agents on real software engineering tasks.

Unlike small code-generation benchmarks, SWE-bench uses real GitHub issues from open-source Python repositories. The model gets an issue description and a codebase, generates a patch, and the result is evaluated by running tests.

This makes it a useful benchmark for checking whether an AI coding agent can do more than generate isolated code snippets.

But running this kind of evaluation reliably is not simple.

You need reproducible environments, automated test runs, a way to compare agent versions, and a way to track metrics like task success rate and cost.

That's what we'll cover in the next workshop: Evaluating AI Coding Agents with TeamCity and SWE-bench

posts.text:
How do I transition from Data engineer to AI engineer?
Here's a structured 6-step transition path:

You already have the hardest part: engineering fundamentals + production mindset.

The goal is to add the AI layer on top.

Step 1: Work inside an AI-flavored data pipeline

- Ingestion + cleaning for RAG / analytics
- Chunking, metadata, indexing
- Observability and data quality checks

Step 2: Learn how model providers work

- APIs, limits, retries, rate limits
- Latency and cost trade-offs
- Privacy and data handling constraints

Step 3: Prompting as an engineering discipline

- Prompt templates
- Versioning + change logs
- Structured outputs (JSON schemas)

Step 4: Evaluation for generative systems

- Golden sets
- Automated checks (format, factuality signals, regressions)
- Human review loops when it matters

Step 5: Tool integration + agentic flows

- Function/tool calling
- Guardrails (allowed tools, timeouts, fallbacks)
- Tracing what the agent did and why

Step 6: Build 1-2 small projects end-to-end

Examples:
- RAG assistant over internal docs
- Ticket triage bot with tool calls + evals

For an experienced data engineer, this is usually not a multi-year shift.

With focused effort + hands-on work, ~3-4 months can be enough to become interview-ready.

If you're making this transition, what part feels most unclear: evals, prompting, or agents?

I'm running the AI Engineering Buildcamp, where we go deeper into agent design, evaluation, monitoring, and guardrails as a system.

This course is a great resource for anyone who considers transitioning into AI Engineer role.

Read more here: https://maven.com/alexey-grigorev/from-rag-to-agents

What are the key skills of an AI engineer?

posts.text:
What are the key skills of an AI engineer?

AI engineer = someone who makes AI testable, observable, versioned, and continuously improving.

Prompting is maybe 5%.
The other 95% is making AI behave reliably after you ship it.

Here are the core skills that separate demos from production:

1) Evaluation + testing

Turn model behavior into something measurable:

- small eval sets (golden questions)
- clear metrics
- regression tests after every change

2) Controlled iteration

Prompts, tools, and models change all the time.

So you need:

- prompt versioning
- experiment tracking (Git / MLflow)
- A/B tests and gradual rollouts

3) Monitoring + observability

If you can't see it, you can't operate it:

- failure types
- latency and cost
- logs + traces for debugging
- alerts when things drift

4) Feedback loops

The best systems improve from real usage:

- ratings and thumbs up/down
- implicit corrections from users
- human review samples
- add bad cases back into the eval set

5) CI/CD for AI

Every change should run evals and block deploys when metrics drop.

6) Product integration

Retries, timeouts, fallbacks, UX edge cases.

I recently did an online session where I explained my view of the role in detail. Recording + notes: https://aishippinglabs.com/blog/what-is-an-ai-engineer-alexey-grigorev-perspective

posts.text:
One principle I strongly believe in and apply in my courses is this: we teach concepts, not tools.

Yes, each course uses specific technologies, but that doesn't mean you're locked into them.

In a recent Q&A about the upcoming Data Engineering Zoomcamp, I shared that the course is designed to teach:

🔸 What workflow orchestration is
🔸 Why data warehousing functions as it does
🔸 How batch and streaming processing differ
🔸 How analytics engineering integrates into the data stack

The tools are just concrete examples.

Prefer Airflow instead of Kestra?
Snowflake or ClickHouse instead of BigQuery?

Totally fine.

Once you understand the underlying concepts, swapping tools becomes a practical decision.

That's also why the course is structured around clear abstractions, transferable mental models, and real-world data engineering workflows.

Tools change, but concepts stay.

posts.text:
We've just started AI Shipping Labs and are still figuring out the format.

Here are the current activities:

1. Accountability circles

You pick a project, join a sprint, and commit to a clear time frame. The group meets for live check-ins. Everyone shares progress, blockers, and next steps. That creates a working rhythm and gives you feedback on both what you're doing and whether you're going in the right direction.

2. Group learning

Members research a topic, test a tool, or explore a concept. Then share findings with the community. Over time, this builds a knowledge base of tested patterns and practical takeaways.

3. Building sessions

Live 1.5 to 2-hour sessions once or twice a month. Topics come from member requests or projects I'm working on. Not a prepared webinar. A working session where we look at a real problem, explore options, and work through trade-offs.

4. Trend breakdowns

We take one trending AI concept, tool, or method and break it down from an engineering perspective: what it is, how it works, why people care, and where to look deeper. Examples: Karpathy's AutoResearch, Mila's AI memory project.

5. Career support

Members discuss interviews, offers, salary questions, LinkedIn, GitHub, and how to present projects. Because the community is private, conversations can be more open. Valeriia also contributes with feedback on positioning and online presence.

We're open to member suggestions and actively listening to their feedback to improve the experience inside the community.

You can learn more about it here: https://aishippinglabs.com/events/ai-shipping-labs-launch-recap?utm_source=x&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=ai_shipping_labs_launch_april2026

posts.text:
I tried using Claude Code as an orchestrator for AI agents team.

Instead of treating it like one coding assistant that does everything, I split the work across 4 roles:

1. The PM turns a raw task into something implementable, with user stories, acceptance criteria, and test scenarios, and then does the final acceptance review from the user’s perspective.

2. The Software Engineer implements the code and writes tests.

3. The Tester runs those tests, checks each acceptance criterion, and reports pass or fail with evidence.

4. The On-Call Engineer watches CI/CD after code is pushed and fixes pipeline failures.

What I like about this setup is that it makes the workflow more explicit.

It becomes harder to skip steps and easier to see where something went wrong.

In my newsletter, I wrote more about how this team works and how I used this approach across several projects.

Read here: https://alexeyondata.substack.com/p/i-built-an-ai-agent-team-for-software

In practice, much of the lifecycle still follows patterns...

posts.text:
LLM systems feel like a new paradigm.

In practice, much of the lifecycle still follows patterns that existed long before generative AI.

One useful lens is CRISP-DM, a framework originally designed for data mining projects and widely adopted in data science.

Even though the tools have changed, its phases map surprisingly well to how modern AI systems are built.

Here is how the typical stages compare.

1. Business Understanding

- Traditional ML: define the prediction task and success metrics.
- AI systems: define the AI-powered product use case and the user experience you want to enable.

2. Data Understanding

- Traditional ML: explore labeled datasets, distributions, and features.
- AI systems: identify the inputs your system will use such as documents, images, APIs, databases, or external tools.

3. Data Preparation

- Traditional ML: feature engineering, cleaning, and dataset curation.
- AI systems: chunking documents, generating embeddings, building indexes, and wiring tools for agents.

4. Modeling

- Traditional ML: train and tune models on structured datasets.
- AI systems: prompt design, schema definition, retrieval pipelines, and agent behavior.

5. Evaluation

- Traditional ML: metrics like accuracy, precision, and recall.
- AI systems: task success, human feedback, and observable system behavior.

6. Deployment

- Traditional ML: model serving and batch or online inference pipelines.
- AI systems: full AI-powered applications that combine models, tools, and orchestration.

The techniques look different, but the lifecycle remains largely the same.

This is one reason many data scientists can smoothly transition into AI engineering roles.

Read more about how CRISP-DM applies to AI Engineering: https://aishippinglabs.com/blog/crisp-dm-for-ai

posts.text:
AI Engineering Buildcamp is project-driven.

You learn AI engineering by building.

15 projects you can build during the course 👇🏼

(You get lifetime access to the course if you sign up)

1. A running example project

A Documentation Agent that evolves throughout the course. It starts as a RAG system and gradually becomes an agent that is tested, monitored, and evaluated.

2. Capstone project

Your own AI application, built step by step during the course, from first RAG version to a more complete system with tools, testing, monitoring, evaluation, and deployment.

Homework projects:

3. Document processing with AI. You download books, extract PDF text, chunk documents, and build a full RAG pipeline.

4. Wikipedia Agent. You implement search and page-fetching tools and build an agent using a framework of your choice.

5. Testing and evaluation through the DuckDB SQL Agent. You build an agent that queries NYC taxi data, write pytest tests, add LLM judges, and track costs.

6. Trivia Quizmaster Agent. You build an interactive trivia system and instrument it with Logfire.

7. Systematic evaluation through the Recipe Assistant Evaluation: You design 20+ evaluation scenarios, run batch tests, and detect hallucinations.

Optional projects:

8. FAQ Assistant: Add search integrations and turn it into a support chatbot.

9. YouTube Transcript Summarizer: A system that extracts summaries and chapter structure from YouTube videos using structured output.

10. PDF Book Processor: Similar tasks often appear in take-home assignments and interviews.

11. Web Search Agent: An agent that uses web search tools to find, filter, and synthesize information from the internet.

12. YouTube Researcher: An agent that searches YouTube, fetches transcripts, and produces structured research summaries.

13. Coding Agent: A fully functional coding agent that scaffolds Django applications.

14. Code Analysis Agent: An agent for analyzing and understanding codebases.

15. Deep Research Agent: A multi-stage research system that starts with broad search, expands into follow-up queries, goes deeper into promising directions, fact-checks findings, and generates a final article.

So you follow one evolving system, practice on separate mini-projects, explore other examples, and build something of your own in parallel.

That is the core of Buildcamp.

The course starts in less than 5 days. You can sign up for the course here: https://maven.com/alexey-grigorev/from-rag-to-agents

posts.text:
People ask about the weekly schedule for AI Engineering Buildcamp.

It's designed for people with full-time jobs: structured, but flexible enough to fit around work.

Here's how much time you'll spend:

The course lasts 9 weeks.

1. Live session - 1 hour per week

We meet for office hours where you can ask technical questions, discuss architecture decisions, and get feedback on your projects.

All sessions are recorded. A written summary is shared a few days later.

2. Async content and homework - 3 to 10 hours per week

Each week includes pre-recorded lessons, practical exercises, and homework. The time depends on your background and pace.

3. Capstone project - ongoing throughout the course

You work on your own AI application from week 1. Each module adds a new layer: RAG, then agentic tools, then testing, monitoring, and evaluation.

By week 6, you'll have a working system. Weeks 7-9 are for polishing, extending, and presenting.

This is not a passive course. It's for people who want to spend real time building and debugging, not just watching and taking notes.

The next cohort starts in less than a week: https://maven.com/alexey-grigorev/from-rag-to-agents

Milla Jovovich (@MillaJovovich) has unexpectedly entered the AI memory conversation with MemPalace, an open-source project she launched with developer Ben Sigman (@bensig).

MemPalace argues that long-term memory for AI assistants does not have to mean more model calls, more infrastructure, and more complexity. It can be local, deterministic, and cheap to run.

The project is inspired by the classical "memory palace" technique: instead of treating memory as a flat retrieval problem, it organizes information into spatial structures.

posts.text:
Basic RAG: you search for a few relevant chunks, pass them to the model, and generate an answer.

That is often a good starting point, but in practice it's not enough for more complex tasks.

Once your application needs to:

- Search multiple times
- Decide what to look for next
- Choose between tools
- Recover from weak intermediate results

you need something more structured than a single retrieve-and-answer step.

At Data Makers Fest 2026, I'll be running a hands-on tutorial on exactly that.

Date: 4 May
Place: Alfândega do Porto, Portugal

You'll learn how to go from a simple RAG system to an agentic search workflow.

If you know Python and have an OpenAI-compatible API key, you'll be able to follow along.

By the end, you'll have a working system and a much clearer picture of how these applications are actually built.

Data Makers Fest is also a good format for this kind of learning. The hands-on tutorials are half-day sessions with small groups, so there's enough time to build, test properly, and understand what's happening.

- Or join the full conference for two days of talks, expo, and networking: https://www.datamakersfest.com/

posts.text:
This is a very important idea.

What stands out to me is the shift from using LLMs as chat interfaces to using them as systems that accumulate, structure, and maintain knowledge over time.

That's very close to what I've been building in my own workflow.

In my case, the raw material is my background work around a project or talk: voice notes, links, screenshots, files, partial thoughts, corrections, and small experiments that happen before anything becomes public.

But the pattern is similar to what @karpathy describes:

Raw inputs come in -> the LLM processes and organizes them -> outputs are stored in a persistent structure -> that structure becomes reusable context for future work.

For me, that became a Telegram-based writing assistant:

- Capture raw ideas in chat
- Transcribe and translate them
- Fetch and summarize links
- Organize images and files
- Update articles incrementally
- Commit everything to GitHub so the workflow has memory and version history

Later, I split parts of the system into subagents for research, resource descriptions, and verification, plus skills for repeated tasks like slide creation.

Example: I can send the assistant a voice note with rough ideas for a talk and ask it to prepare slides.

It'll process my voice note. Then, it can also find related material in my repo, like an earlier Markdown article on the same topic, process both sources together, combine them into a presentation structure, and fill in the content.

That's very close to what Karpathy describes: a workflow where the knowledge base itself becomes an active working environment for future research and creation.

posts.text:
The Telegram Writing Assistant
It is a custom, automated system built with Claude Code agents that acts as a bridge between raw, messy ideas and finished content. It takes invisible "background work" and transforms it into structured Markdown drafts stored directly in a GitHub repository.

What It Can Do
Process Multimodal Inputs: Accepts text messages, voice notes, standard audio files, images, and even YouTube links directly in a private Telegram chat.

Transcribe & Translate: Automatically converts audio to text (via Whisper) and translates on the fly (e.g., turning Russian voice notes into English text).

Summarize External Content: Fetches URLs, technical documentation, and YouTube transcripts, extracting key insights to seamlessly integrate into drafts.

Delegate via Subagents: Uses specialized AI subagents to prevent context overload:

Article-summarizer: Digests heavy research links.

Resource-describer: Writes brief blurbs for curated links.

Verify-content: Double-checks drafts to ensure no nuanced details from the original voice notes were lost.

Automate with "Skills": Executes repeatable workflows, such as updating its own configuration based on feedback or auto-generating presentation slides.

What I Use It For
Frictionless Brain Dumping: Capturing fleeting thoughts, experiments, and corrections on the go without worrying about manual sorting.

Drafting Articles & Newsletters: Automatically categorizing and stitching my scattered ideas into polished pieces for my Substack.

Curating Weekly Resources: Instantly generating short, accurate descriptions for tools and links I want to feature in my newsletter.

Building Workshop Materials: Dictating raw concepts into the chat and using custom Claude skills to iteratively generate and refine presentation slides.

posts.text:
What are skills in AI agents?

In one of the workshops, I demo a GitHub Fetch skill.

The task seems simple: retrieve files from a GitHub repository. But without this skill, the agent must guess how to:

- Interact with GitHub
- Choose the right commands
- Navigate the repository structure

A skill provides a reusable set of instructions that guides the agent through tasks step by step.

Specifically, the GitHub Fetch skill instructs the agent on:

- Using the gh CLI
- Listing repository contents
- Navigating directories
- Downloading specific files

With these validated instructions, skills minimize reasoning errors by encoding operational knowledge.

In the demo, we used this skill to fetch two commands from a GitHub repo:

- /kid generates a wild project idea
- /parent implements it as code

These commands are stored in GitHub, and the agent uses the GitHub Fetch skill to automatically retrieve them.

Skills offer benefits like:

- Making behavior predictable
- Avoiding repeated prompts
- Reusing hard-won instructions
- Scaling beyond one-off demos

I teach how to build production-ready AI agents in my AI Bootcamp. We go deeper into agent design, evaluation, monitoring, and guardrails as a system.

posts.text:
When building agents, what is the difference between skills and commands?
They look similar, but they serve different roles.

1. Commands are explicit. You can think of them as user-driven shortcuts

🔸 The user knows exactly what should happen
🔸 The user triggers it directly, for example /kit
🔸 The agent simply executes the instruction

2. Skills are implicit

🔸 The user describes a task in natural language
🔸 The agent decides whether a skill applies
🔸 The agent loads and uses the skill autonomously

The user never says, "Use this skill"

Skills encode operational knowledge. They tell the agent how to do something, so it doesn't have to guess.

3. The key distinction is who makes the decision:

🔸 Commands: the user decides
🔸 Skills: the agent decides

Commands are best when the intent is precise.

Skills are better when you want reusable, predictable agent behavior across tasks and projects.

If you want to go deeper, I've shared a free workshop on implementing skills from scratch:

🔸 Video: https://youtu.be/OhgDEZfHsvg
🔸 Code: https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/workshops/tree/main/agent-skills

I also teach how to build production-ready AI agents in my AI Engineering Buildcamp. We go deeper into agent design, evaluation, monitoring, and guardrails as a system.

posts.text:
What are guardrails for AI agents?
Here's a simple way to think about them:

1. What are guardrails?

Guardrails are mechanisms that control how the model reacts to user input and what the user ultimately sees.

2. Why are guardrails important?

An agent will try to be helpful, even when it shouldn't.

For example, imagine an agent built to answer questions about a course.

Without guardrails:
🔸 A student can ask for pizza recipes
🔸 The agent will try to answer
🔸 You spend tokens and money on completely off-topic requests

Guardrails prevent this.

They let you define what is allowed and what is not, before or after the model responds.

3. In practice, guardrails help you:

🔸 Block off-topic questions early
🔸 Refuse requests you don't want to support
🔸 Avoid unsafe or inappropriate outputs
🔸 Save money by stopping useless calls

You decide what the agent is for. Guardrails enforce that decision.

Once agents are exposed to real users, guardrails stop being optional. They become part of the system design.

I walk through this step by step in a free workshop:

Video: https://youtu.be/Sk1aqwNJWT4?si=T6afVvKelro438OQ
Code: https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/workshops/tree/main/guardrails

This workshop is also a preview of the AI Engineering Buildcamp, where we go deeper into agent design, evaluation, monitoring, and guardrails as a system.

posts.text:
4 key components of AI agent architecture in its simplest form:

1. Brain: The LLM. It reasons, plans, and decides what to do next.

2. Instructions: The system prompt. It defines the agent's role, boundaries, and behavior.

3. Tools: Functions the agent can call to interact with the world:
reading files, writing code, running commands, searching data.

4. Memory: The conversation history and tool results that provide context across steps.

How this works together is what people call the agentic loop:

🔸 The user gives a task
🔸 The agent reasons based on instructions and memory
🔸 It decides to respond or call a tool
🔸 Tool results are added to memory
🔸 The loop continues until the task is complete

The agent decides when to stop.

Once you see this loop clearly, agent frameworks become much easier to reason about. They're mostly different ways of wiring these same components together.

If you want a hands-on walkthrough of this architecture, I've shared free workshop materials.

🔸 Video: https://youtu.be/OhgDEZfHsvg
🔸 Code: https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/workshops/tree/main/agent-skills

posts.text:
I recently ran a workshop on building safe AI agents with guardrails.

One part of it focuses on building a search engine for a real FAQ before adding any agent logic.

The example uses a large FAQ for a Data Engineering course hosted on GitHub: 300+ questions, written by students.

We go through this step by step:

🔸 Fetch the FAQ data directly from GitHub
🔸 Parse questions and answers into a clean Python structure
🔸 Index the content to make it searchable
🔸 Verify that search returns relevant results

Only after that do we add an agent on top.

Retrieval and data grounding are important parts of an agent's design, because an agent is only as good as its access to data.

If retrieval is weak, the agent will confidently answer incorrectly.

My workshop shows how to ground an agent in real, verifiable data before adding guardrails and agentic behavior.

Here are the materials:

Video: https://youtu.be/Sk1aqwNJWT4?si=T6afVvKelro438OQ
Code: https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/workshops/tree/main/guardrails

posts.text:
Developer cheatsheet to turn a chatbot into a coding agent:

1) Chatbot vs agent decision

Decide upfront whether you actually need an agent. Agents are only worth it when you need actions like file I/O, code execution, or search.

2) Tool schema definition

Define concrete tools with strict schemas describing names, parameters, and constraints, and expose only what the agent should be allowed to do.

3) Tool execution loop

Implement a loop where the model proposes tool calls, your system executes them, and the results are fed back into the conversation state.

4) Project-scoped editing tools

Provide file and shell access scoped to a project root, with guardrails to prevent unsafe commands and accidental damage.

5) Project template scaffolding

Start each run from a clean template copied into a fresh directory so all agent edits remain isolated and reproducible.

6) System prompt as documentation

Use the system prompt to document the tech stack, file structure, and rules, and require the model to plan before acting.

Use this as a checklist when building a tool-using coding agent on top of your preferred stack and LLM API.

Want a detailed step-by-step tutorial? Download my guide here: https://maven.com/p/f2d4cd/build-your-own-coding-agent-free-guide

posts.text:
How to connect AI agents to tools?

Here's an example from a recent workshop where I built an FAQ assistant that answers student questions based on an FAQ document.

We start with a simple Python search function that queries an indexed FAQ.

The key step is turning that function into a tool and giving it to an agent.

Here's how to do it:

🔸 Define a search function over the FAQ index
🔸 Decorate it as a tool so the agent can call it
🔸 Create an agent with clear system instructions
🔸 Assign the tool to the agent

In my case, instructions tell the agent:

🔸 You are a teaching assistant
🔸 Your job is to answer questions using the FAQ
🔸 Use the search tool when needed

When a user asks a question, the agent:

🔸 Decides whether to call the tool
🔸 Generates a search query
🔸 Inspects the returned results
🔸 Produces the final answer

You can inspect every tool call to see exactly how the agent reasons and why it chose a particular answer.

This material comes from a free workshop on building safe AI agents, where we go from search to agents and then add guardrails on top.

Materials:

Video: https://youtu.be/Sk1aqwNJWT4?si=T6afVvKelro438OQ
Code: https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/workshops/tree/main/guardrails

posts.text:
What does AI Engineering Buildcamp cover?

It'll teach you to build and ship your own agentic AI assistant, from first prompt to production-ready system:

1. Foundations: LLMs and RAG

We start with core concepts and move quickly into implementation.

You learn how to:

🔸 Work with LLM APIs
🔸 Build retrieval-augmented generation pipelines
🔸 Process and structure real data

Outcome: a working RAG system built on your own dataset.

2. Agentic Flows and Tool Use

Next, we move beyond chat.

You implement:

🔸 Function calling
🔸 Tool integration with structured schemas
🔸 Agent orchestration with libraries like PydanticAI and Agents SDK
🔸 Tool exposure via MCP

Outcome: a capable, tool-using agent that can take actions, not just generate text.

3. Testing and Evaluation

Most AI demos stop at “it works.”

We focus on making it measurable.

You learn how to:

posts.text:
Something I've been finding useful recently: using Claude Code not as a single coding assistant, but as an orchestrator for a small software team. For simple tools, one agent is often enough. For larger projects, it becomes harder to track what is done, verify that it matches the plan, and catch false claims of completion. Splitting the work into roles has been a better way to handle that. So:

Team structure:
I split the work across four roles. The Product Manager turns a raw idea into an implementable spec with user stories, acceptance criteria, and test scenarios, and later does the final acceptance review from the user's perspective. The Software Engineer implements the code and writes tests. The Tester runs those tests, checks the acceptance criteria, and reports pass or fail with evidence. The On-Call Engineer monitors CI/CD after code is pushed and fixes pipeline failures.

Pipeline:
Every task follows the same sequence. The orchestrator creates the task and adds it to the backlog. The PM grooms it. The SWE implements it. QA verifies it. If QA rejects the task, it goes back to the SWE for fixes. If QA accepts it, the PM does a final acceptance review. Only after that does the orchestrator commit the code and close the task. That final PM review matters because passing tests is not enough. A feature can be technically correct and still miss the original user story.

Process encoding:
To keep the workflow consistent, I write it down in the repository. .claude/agents/ contains the role definitions. PROCESS.md describes the workflow. CLAUDE.md contains project-level instructions. The execute skill starts the pipeline. This gives the agents a shared process instead of relying on repeated instructions in chat.

Task tracking:
For tracking, I use either GitHub Issues or a file-based tracker. GitHub works well when I want visible coordination and reports attached to each task. The file-based approach is lighter: task status is encoded in the filename, moving from .todo.md to .groomed.md to .in-progress.md, and eventually into done/. The tool matters less than preserving the workflow. In both cases, the same PM -> SWE -> QA -> PM loop stays in place.

Parallel work:
I usually run two tasks in parallel. When that batch is finished, the orchestrator pulls the next two from the backlog. To keep this going without manual intervention, I keep a recurring instruction in the task list telling the orchestrator to fetch the next batch and then re-add the same instruction. That keeps the process moving until the backlog is empty.

Why this helps:
The main benefit is narrower responsibility. It becomes harder to skip steps and easier to see where something went wrong. It also avoids a common failure mode where the same agent writes the code and decides that it is correct. Separating planning, implementation, testing, and acceptance makes the process easier to control.

Limits:
This is still a work in progress. The orchestrator sometimes stops when it should continue, asks for confirmation when work is still queued, or skips the intended flow and starts implementation directly. Visibility into subagents is also limited. So the setup still needs supervision.

Projects:
I've tested this setup across five software projects. The main pattern stays the same: define the roles, define the pipeline, let the orchestrator move tasks through it, and step in only when needed. That has been enough to show that the approach is useful, but also that prompt-based enforcement has clear limits.

Further explorations:
The next step is to move more of the methodology out of markdown files and into software. Right now, the process is written as instructions the agent can ignore. What I want instead is an orchestrator where the workflow itself is enforced by the tool: PM grooming, SWE implementation, QA verification, PM acceptance, and only then commit. I also want better visibility into subagents, support for multiple backends, and a non-blocking task pool.

TLDR:
Instead of using Claude Code as one coding assistant, I use it as an orchestrator for a small team of agents with distinct roles: PM, SWE, QA, and on-call. Every task moves through the same pipeline from backlog to grooming, implementation, verification, final acceptance, and only then commit. The process is written down in the repo so the agents can follow it consistently. It still needs supervision, but for complex projects it works better than a single-agent chat loop.

posts.text:
5 main AI agent evaluation dimensions:

1. Goal -> Action
2. Goal -> Plan
3. Plan -> Action
4. End-to-end consistency
5. Efficiency

🧵

1. Goal -> Action

Did the agent complete the task correctly?

This includes classic metrics like correctness, relevance, and grounding or faithfulness to retrieved context or knowledge sources.

2. Goal -> Plan

Was the plan good enough to achieve the goal?

Here you evaluate whether the agent chose the right approach, selected the right tools, and arranged them in a reasonable sequence.

3. Plan -> Action

Did execution actually follow the plan?

This helps you see whether the agent used the tools it intended to use, whether it deviated, and whether it passed valid and sensible inputs into those tools.

4. End-to-end consistency

Was the agent logically consistent across the whole trace?

This captures cases where the agent says one thing, does another, ignores its own plan, or drifts away from the original instructions.

5. Efficiency

Did the agent use tools efficiently?

This includes redundant calls, unnecessary repetition, and extra steps that increase cost and latency without improving the result.

This is the main idea: evaluating only the final output is not enough for agentic systems.

If you want to understand why an agent fails and how to improve it, you need to inspect the process itself, not just the ending.

For a deeper practical look at evaluating MCP-powered agents, watch our @Snowflake workshop with @_jreini: https://www.youtube.com/live/oMmJvlNuDZE?si=jhW4n937fdkbQmpF

He walks through the Agent GPA (Goal-Plan-Action) framework, available in the open-source TruLens library.
