posts.text:
How to evaluate AI agents step-by-step?

1. Verify goal understanding
2. Assess plan quality
3. Inspect tool execution
4. Compare plan and execution
5. Evaluate replanning
6. Measure efficiency
7. Review end-to-end consistency

🧵

1. Verify goal understanding

Check whether the agent correctly interpreted the user’s request, including constraints and success criteria. If the goal is misunderstood, later steps are unlikely to be reliable.

2. Assess plan quality

Review whether the proposed plan could reasonably achieve the goal. This includes step selection, tool choice, and step order.

3. Inspect tool execution

Examine each tool call for relevance and correctness. Check whether the agent used the right tool, passed valid inputs, and made use of the returned output appropriately.

4. Compare plan and execution

Determine whether the agent followed its plan. If it deviated, assess whether the deviation was justified by new information or tool results.

5. Evaluate replanning

When conditions changed or errors occurred, check whether the agent updated its approach in a coherent way rather than continuing blindly or switching direction without logic.

6. Measure efficiency

Look for unnecessary steps, redundant tool calls, repeated searches, or avoidable latency and cost.

7. Review end-to-end consistency

Assess whether the goal, plan, actions, and final response remain aligned throughout the trace. This helps identify cases where the agent produced a plausible answer through weak or inconsistent reasoning.

For a deeper practical look at evaluating MCP-powered agents, watch our @Snowflake workshop with @_jreini: https://www.youtube.com/live/oMmJvlNuDZE?si=jhW4n937fdkbQmpF

He walks through the Agent GPA (Goal-Plan-Action) framework, available in the open-source TruLens library.

How to evaluate AI agents step-by-step?
A common mistake in agent evaluation is to assess only the final answer.

For tool-using agents, that is often insufficient.

The main failure modes usually appear in the execution process: how the agent interprets the goal, builds a plan, uses tools, adapts to new information, and decides when to stop.

A practical evaluation process should review the full trace.

1. Verify goal understanding

Check whether the agent correctly interpreted the user’s request, including constraints and success criteria. If the goal is misunderstood, later steps are unlikely to be reliable.

2. Assess plan quality

Review whether the proposed plan could reasonably achieve the goal. This includes step selection, tool choice, and step order.

3. Inspect tool execution

Examine each tool call for relevance and correctness. Check whether the agent used the right tool, passed valid inputs, and made use of the returned output appropriately.

4. Compare plan and execution

Determine whether the agent followed its plan. If it deviated, assess whether the deviation was justified by new information or tool results.

5. Evaluate replanning

When conditions changed or errors occurred, check whether the agent updated its approach in a coherent way rather than continuing blindly or switching direction without logic.

6. Measure efficiency

Look for unnecessary steps, redundant tool calls, repeated searches, or avoidable latency and cost.

7. Review end-to-end consistency

Assess whether the goal, plan, actions, and final response remain aligned throughout the trace. This helps identify cases where the agent produced a plausible answer through weak or inconsistent reasoning.

That gives a more reliable view of agent quality and makes it easier to identify concrete areas for improvement.

My Telegram Writing Assistant started as a simple bot that turned voice notes into Markdown drafts.

Over time, it grew into a larger workflow: processing external links, summarizing long articles, organizing research, and preparing newsletter resources.

That also exposed a limitation. One agent was doing too much inside a single context window. As more URLs and messages were processed together, the workflow became slower, less predictable, and more likely to lose detail.

In my new newsletter, I write about how I refactored this system using Claude Code subagents and skills.

I cover:

- Why the single-agent setup stopped working well
- How I split the workflow into separate agents for research, link descriptions, and verification
- Why I added a verification step for voice-note-based content
- New support for audio files and YouTube transcripts
- How I use Claude Code skills for repeated tasks like slide creation

Read it here: https://alexeyondata.substack.com/p/i-turned-my-telegram-bot-into-a-multi

How do AI Engineering, ML Engineering, and Data Science relate?

They all touch models, evaluation,...

posts.text:
How do AI Engineering, ML Engineering, and Data Science relate?

They all touch models, evaluation, deployment, and iteration.
But the center of gravity differs.

1. Data Science = build the model

- Turn business problems into ML tasks
- Create datasets
- Train, test, validate

2. ML Engineering = ship the model

- Integrate into systems
- Manage infra, deployments, versions
- Keep it reliable and scalable

3. AI Engineering = ship AI (often via APIs)
Most teams don't train foundation models. They use OpenAI/Anthropic/Google.

So the bottleneck shifts: from training to engineering:

- System integration
- Prompt design + versioning
- Output structuring
- Eval frameworks
- Monitoring, cost control
- Operational reliability

In short:

- Data Science optimizes the model.
- ML Engineering productionizes it.
- AI Engineering operationalizes third‑party intelligence inside a product.

More detail (recording + notes):
https://aishippinglabs.com/blog/what-is-an-ai-engineer-alexey-grigorev-perspective

If you work in one of these roles, where do you see the boundaries in practice?

How do AI Engineering, ML Engineering, and Data Science relate?

They all touch models, evaluation, deployment, and iteration.
But the center of gravity differs.

1. Data Science = build the model

- Turn business problems into ML tasks
- Create datasets
- Train, test, validate

2. ML Engineering = ship the model

- Integrate into systems
- Manage infra, deployments, versions
- Keep it reliable and scalable

3. AI Engineering = ship AI (often via APIs)
Most teams don't train foundation models. They use OpenAI/Anthropic/Google.

So the bottleneck shifts: from training to engineering:

- System integration
- Prompt design + versioning
- Output structuring
- Eval frameworks
- Monitoring, cost control
- Operational reliability

In short:

- Data Science optimizes the model.
- ML Engineering productionizes it.
- AI Engineering operationalizes third‑party intelligence inside a product.

LLM systems feel like a new paradigm.

In practice, much of the lifecycle still follows patterns...

posts.text:
LLM systems feel like a new paradigm.

In practice, much of the lifecycle still follows patterns that existed long before generative AI.

One useful lens is CRISP-DM, a framework originally designed for data mining projects and widely adopted in data science.

Even though the tools have changed, its phases map surprisingly well to how modern AI systems are built.

Here is how the typical stages compare.

1. Business Understanding

- Traditional ML: define the prediction task and success metrics.
- AI systems: define the AI-powered product use case and the user experience you want to enable.

2. Data Understanding

- Traditional ML: explore labeled datasets, distributions, and features.
- AI systems: identify the inputs your system will use such as documents, images, APIs, databases, or external tools.

3. Data Preparation

- Traditional ML: feature engineering, cleaning, and dataset curation.
- AI systems: chunking documents, generating embeddings, building indexes, and wiring tools for agents.

4. Modeling

- Traditional ML: train and tune models on structured datasets.
- AI systems: prompt design, schema definition, retrieval pipelines, and agent behavior.

5. Evaluation

- Traditional ML: metrics like accuracy, precision, and recall.
- AI systems: task success, human feedback, and observable system behavior.

6. Deployment

- Traditional ML: model serving and batch or online inference pipelines.
- AI systems: full AI-powered applications that combine models, tools, and orchestration.

The techniques look different, but the lifecycle remains largely the same.

This is one reason many data scientists can smoothly transition into AI engineering roles.

Read more about how CRISP-DM applies to AI Engineering: https://aishippinglabs.com/blog/crisp-dm-for-ai

payload.preview: When building AI agents, it's common to test them by asking a question and checking whether the...

posts.text:
When building AI agents, it's common to test them by asking a question and checking whether the answer looks correct.

But the final answer alone doesn't tell you much about how the agent behaved.

An agent might:

- Skip a tool it should have used
- Choose the wrong tool
- Call the right tool with incorrect parameters
- Rely on the model’s internal knowledge instead of external data

To understand these behaviors, you need observability and structured evaluation.

Instead of looking only at outputs, you analyze the execution traces of the agent:

- Which tools it called
- How it reasoned
- How it used external data

From these traces you can compute metrics such as tool selection or tool calling quality and compare different versions of the agent.

This type of workflow makes it possible to identify concrete failure modes and improve the system iteratively.

If you're interested in how this works in practice, we're running a hands-on workshop where we'll build an agent, evaluate it, and improve it step by step.

How do I transition from Data engineer to AI engineer?
Here's a structured 6-step transition...

posts.text:
How do I transition from Data engineer to AI engineer?
Here's a structured 6-step transition path:

You already have the hardest part: engineering fundamentals + production mindset.

The goal is to add the AI layer on top.

Step 1: Work inside an AI-flavored data pipeline

- Ingestion + cleaning for RAG / analytics
- Chunking, metadata, indexing
- Observability and data quality checks

Step 2: Learn how model providers work

- APIs, limits, retries, rate limits
- Latency and cost trade-offs
- Privacy and data handling constraints

Step 3: Prompting as an engineering discipline

- Prompt templates
- Versioning + change logs
- Structured outputs (JSON schemas)

Step 4: Evaluation for generative systems

- Golden sets
- Automated checks (format, factuality signals, regressions)
- Human review loops when it matters

Step 5: Tool integration + agentic flows

- Function/tool calling
- Guardrails (allowed tools, timeouts, fallbacks)
- Tracing what the agent did and why

Step 6: Build 1-2 small projects end-to-end

Examples:
- RAG assistant over internal docs
- Ticket triage bot with tool calls + evals

For an experienced data engineer, this is usually not a multi-year shift.

With focused effort + hands-on work, ~3-4 months can be enough to become interview-ready.

If you're making this transition, what part feels most unclear: evals, prompting, or agents?

I'm running the AI Engineering Buildcamp, where we go deeper into agent design, evaluation, monitoring, and guardrails as a system.

This course is a great resource for anyone who considers transitioning into AI Engineer role.

Read more here: https://maven.com/alexey-grigorev/from-rag-to-agents

Karpathy's autoresearch project has been everywhere lately.

I spent some time going through the...

posts.text:
Karpathy's autoresearch project has been everywhere lately.

I spent some time going through the repo to understand what it actually does.

The core idea is surprisingly simple: an agent edits the training code, runs an experiment, checks a metric, and keeps the change only if the result improves. Then it repeats the loop.

In Karpathy's example, the system made 110 successful changes in ~12 hours.

What I find most interesting is the structure:

- prepare.py defines the rules and evaluation metric
- train.py is the code the agent modifies
- program.md is where the human writes instructions in natural language

So the workflow becomes:

1. A human writes instructions
2. LLM writes Python
3. Python trains the model

Instead of directly improving the model, you're programming the research process using natural language.

If you're curious how the loop works and why people are experimenting with it, I wrote a short breakdown: https://alexeyondata.substack.com/p/karpathys-autoresearch-went-viral

In the post, I also share one idea this pattern could be used for: automatically optimizing writing-style prompts.

posts.text:
Can a data engineer transition into AI engineering?

Short answer: yes. And in many cases, faster than they think.

AI engineering is primarily an engineering role.

There is far less research and model training than people assume. In modern AI systems, the foundation model is usually an API call. The hard part is everything around it.

If you are a data engineer, you already have the core.

You know how to:

- Write tests
- Set up CI/CD
- Monitor pipelines
- Collect logs
- Follow solid engineering practices

The "flavor" changes, but the fundamentals stay the same.

Instead of data quality monitoring, you monitor AI behavior.
Instead of batch pipelines, you may manage RAG pipelines.
Instead of validating transformations, you evaluate model outputs.

But these are extensions of what you already do.

I'm running the AI Engineering Buildcamp, where we go deeper into agent design, evaluation, monitoring, and guardrails as a system.

This course is a great resource for anyone who considers transitioning into AI Engineer role.

Read more here: https://maven.com/alexey-grigorev/from-rag-to-agents

posts.text:
What does the weekly schedule of AI Engineering Buildcamp look like?

It is designed for working professionals. Structured, but flexible.

Here is how the time is distributed.

1. Live session
⏱ 1 hour per week

We meet once a week for office hours.

You can:

🔸 Ask technical questions
🔸 Clarify architectural decisions
🔸 Discuss your project
🔸 Dive deeper into tricky topics

All sessions are recorded.
A written summary is shared a few days later.

If you cannot attend live, you do not miss anything.

2. Async content and homework
⏱ 3 to 10 hours per week

Each week includes:

🔸 Pre-recorded lectures
🔸 Hands-on exercises
🔸 Structured homework

The time depends on your pace and background.

The focus is practical. You implement, test, iterate.

3. Final project
⏱ 10 to 20 hours per week

The capstone project runs throughout the course.

You progressively build an end-to-end AI application using what you learn each week.

By the end, you are not starting from scratch.
You are polishing and integrating components you have already built.

The effort increases toward the final weeks, but it is distributed across the entire duration.

In total, expect a meaningful time commitment.

This is not a passive course.

It is designed to simulate real AI engineering work:

🔸 Build
🔸 Evaluate
🔸 Monitor
🔸 Improve

You can join the next cohort here: https://maven.com/alexey-grigorev/from-rag-to-agents

Tomorrow I'll run an in-person Exasol workshop in Berlin.

During the session, we'll work with UK NHS prescription data: more than 1 billion prescription records.

We'll build a complete pipeline from raw data to analytics, then automate it using Kestra.

What we'll do:

- Deploy Exasol Personal Edition on AWS
- Explore a public healthcare dataset with prescription records from UK GP practices
- Load raw CSV files into Exasol and transform them into warehouse tables
- Automate the loading steps using Python scripts
- Use Kestra to orchestrate the pipeline across multiple months of data

posts.text:
What does AI Engineering Buildcamp cover?

It'll teach you to build and ship your own agentic AI assistant, from first prompt to production-ready system:

1. Foundations: LLMs and RAG

We start with core concepts and move quickly into implementation.

You learn how to:

🔸 Work with LLM APIs
🔸 Build retrieval-augmented generation pipelines
🔸 Process and structure real data

Outcome: a working RAG system built on your own dataset.

2. Agentic Flows and Tool Use

Next, we move beyond chat.

You implement:

🔸 Function calling
🔸 Tool integration with structured schemas
🔸 Agent orchestration with libraries like PydanticAI and Agents SDK
🔸 Tool exposure via MCP

Outcome: a capable, tool-using agent that can take actions, not just generate text.

3. Testing and Evaluation

Most AI demos stop at “it works.”

We focus on making it measurable.

You learn how to:

🔸 Build structured evaluation datasets
🔸 Compare approaches using LLMs as judges
🔸 Run offline evaluation
🔸 Use tools like Evidently and LangWatch

Outcome: a tested and benchmarked assistant.

4. Monitoring and Guardrails

Production systems require observability and safety.

You implement:

🔸 Real-time monitoring with Grafana
🔸 Structured logging with Pydantic Logfire
🔸 OpenTelemetry instrumentation
🔸 Guardrails and safety mechanisms

Outcome: a monitored system you can operate with confidence.

5. Applied Use Cases

You build concrete agents, including:

🔸 A website generator
🔸 A code reviewer

You also explore additional real-world scenarios to understand architectural trade-offs.

6. Capstone and Hackathon

Everything comes together.

You build a complete end-to-end AI application using your own data.

Then you apply the stack in a hackathon setting, solving real problems collaboratively.

Outcome: a portfolio-ready project that demonstrates real AI engineering skills.

By the end of the Buildcamp, you will:

🔸 Build, evaluate, and monitor an AI assistant
🔸 Create research and coding agents
🔸 Understand the full lifecycle from prototype to production
🔸 Have a concrete project to show in interviews

Join the next cohort here: https://maven.com/alexey-grigorev/from-rag-to-agents

How do I transition from Data engineer to AI engineer?
Here's a structured 6-step transition...

posts.text:
How do I transition from Data engineer to AI engineer?
Here's a structured 6-step transition path:

You already have the hardest part: engineering fundamentals + production mindset.

The goal is to add the AI layer on top.

Step 1: Work inside an AI-flavored data pipeline

- Ingestion + cleaning for RAG / analytics
- Chunking, metadata, indexing
- Observability and data quality checks

Step 2: Learn how model providers work

- APIs, limits, retries, rate limits
- Latency and cost trade-offs
- Privacy and data handling constraints

Step 3: Prompting as an engineering discipline

- Prompt templates
- Versioning + change logs
- Structured outputs (JSON schemas)

Step 4: Evaluation for generative systems

- Golden sets
- Automated checks (format, factuality signals, regressions)
- Human review loops when it matters

Step 5: Tool integration + agentic flows

- Function/tool calling
- Guardrails (allowed tools, timeouts, fallbacks)
- Tracing what the agent did and why

Step 6: Build 1-2 small projects end-to-end

Examples:
- RAG assistant over internal docs
- Ticket triage bot with tool calls + evals

For an experienced data engineer, this is usually not a multi-year shift.

With focused effort + hands-on work, ~3-4 months can be enough to become interview-ready.

If you're making this transition, what part feels most unclear: evals, prompting, or agents?

I'm running the AI Engineering Buildcamp, where we go deeper into agent design, evaluation, monitoring, and guardrails as a system.

This course is a great resource for anyone who considers transitioning into AI Engineer role.

Read more here: https://maven.com/alexey-grigorev/from-rag-to-agents

posts.text:
What are the key skills of an AI engineer?

AI engineer = someone who makes AI testable, observable, versioned, and continuously improving.

Prompting is maybe 5%.
The other 95% is making AI behave reliably after you ship it.

Here are the core skills that separate demos from production:

1) Evaluation + testing

Turn model behavior into something measurable:

- small eval sets (golden questions)
- clear metrics
- regression tests after every change

2) Controlled iteration

Prompts, tools, and models change all the time.

So you need:

- prompt versioning
- experiment tracking (Git / MLflow)
- A/B tests and gradual rollouts

3) Monitoring + observability

If you can't see it, you can't operate it:

- failure types
- latency and cost
- logs + traces for debugging
- alerts when things drift

4) Feedback loops

The best systems improve from real usage:

- ratings and thumbs up/down
- implicit corrections from users
- human review samples
- add bad cases back into the eval set

5) CI/CD for AI

Every change should run evals and block deploys when metrics drop.

6) Product integration

Retries, timeouts, fallbacks, UX edge cases.

I recently did an online session where I explained my view of the role in detail. Recording + notes: https://aishippinglabs.com/blog/what-is-an-ai-engineer-alexey-grigorev-perspective

posts.text:
How do you tell an AI hobbyist from an AI engineer?

The difference is about standards. An AI engineer follows engineering discipline.

That means:

- Writing proper tests
- Defining measurable evaluation criteria
- Monitoring performance and cost
- Collecting feedback
- Making data-driven decisions
- Designing for maintainability

A hobbyist can make something work.

An engineer makes it reliable.

For personal use, when you take on the AI hobbist role, you do not need:

- A comprehensive test suite
- Monitoring dashboards
- Structured evaluation pipelines
- Versioning and rollback strategies

You just run it. If it works, great. If not, you tweak it.

In a company setting, that is not enough.

When AI is integrated into a product, you need:

- Reproducibility
- Observability
- Clear evaluation
- Controlled iteration

I'm running the AI Engineering Buildcamp, where we go deeper into agent design, evaluation, monitoring, and guardrails as a system.

This course is a great resource for anyone who considers transitioning into AI Engineer role.

posts.text:
Can a data engineer transition into AI engineering?

Short answer: yes. And in many cases, faster than they think.

AI engineering is primarily an engineering role.

There is far less research and model training than people assume. In modern AI systems, the foundation model is usually an API call. The hard part is everything around it.

If you are a data engineer, you already have the core.

You know how to:

- Write tests
- Set up CI/CD
- Monitor pipelines
- Collect logs
- Follow solid engineering practices

The "flavor" changes, but the fundamentals stay the same.

Instead of data quality monitoring, you monitor AI behavior.
Instead of batch pipelines, you may manage RAG pipelines.
Instead of validating transformations, you evaluate model outputs.

But these are extensions of what you already do.

This course is a great resource for anyone who considers transitioning into AI Engineer role.

posts.text:
How to connect AI agents to tools?

Here's an example from a recent workshop where I built an FAQ assistant that answers student questions based on an FAQ document.

We start with a simple Python search function that queries an indexed FAQ.

The key step is turning that function into a tool and giving it to an agent.

Here's how to do it:

🔸 Define a search function over the FAQ index
🔸 Decorate it as a tool so the agent can call it
🔸 Create an agent with clear system instructions
🔸 Assign the tool to the agent

In my case, instructions tell the agent:

🔸 You are a teaching assistant
🔸 Your job is to answer questions using the FAQ
🔸 Use the search tool when needed

When a user asks a question, the agent:

🔸 Decides whether to call the tool
🔸 Generates a search query
🔸 Inspects the returned results
🔸 Produces the final answer

You can inspect every tool call to see exactly how the agent reasons and why it chose a particular answer.

This material comes from a free workshop on building safe AI agents, where we go from search to agents and then add guardrails on top.

Materials:

Video: https://youtu.be/Sk1aqwNJWT4?si=T6afVvKelro438OQ
Code: https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/workshops/tree/main/guardrails

The core idea is atomicity: each component does one thing well and composes cleanly with others.

Every agent, tool, and context provider is:

- Reusable: Works across multiple pipelines
- Composable: Combines easily with other components

If you're tired of bloated frameworks and want modular, maintainable AI pipelines, this is worth exploring.

posts.text:
Over the past year, AI Engineer and GenAI Engineer titles have appeared much more frequently on job boards and LinkedIn profiles.

But what does it actually mean?

After 15 years in software engineering and 12 years building ML systems in production, here's my definition:

AI engineer is responsible for integrating AI into the product.

Building and operating AI-powered systems in production to make sure the AI part:

- Runs reliably
- Can be evaluated
- Can be maintained
- Can be improved over time

In other words, the AI engineer owns the AI layer of the product.

What does an AI Engineer actually do?

The responsibilities typically include:

- Translating product requirements into well-scoped AI problems
- Selecting and integrating foundation models and tools
- Crafting and versioning prompts
- Defining success metrics and building proper test suites
- Managing deployment and monitoring performance
- Handling cost optimization
- Implementing security measures

posts.text:
How do AI Engineering, ML Engineering, and Data Science relate?

They all touch models, evaluation, deployment, and iteration.
But the center of gravity differs.

1. Data Science = build the model

- Turn business problems into ML tasks
- Create datasets
- Train, test, validate

2. ML Engineering = ship the model

- Integrate into systems
- Manage infra, deployments, versions
- Keep it reliable and scalable

3. AI Engineering = ship AI (often via APIs)
Most teams don't train foundation models. They use OpenAI/Anthropic/Google.

So the bottleneck shifts: from training to engineering:

- System integration
- Prompt design + versioning
- Output structuring
- Eval frameworks
- Monitoring, cost control
- Operational reliability

In short:

- Data Science optimizes the model.
- ML Engineering productionizes it.
- AI Engineering operationalizes third‑party intelligence inside a product.

More detail (recording + notes):
https://aishippinglabs.com/blog/what-is-an-ai-engineer-alexey-grigorev-perspective

payload.preview: Most coding assistants today fall into a few categories: chat-based assistants, IDE agents, CLI...

posts.text:
Most coding assistants today fall into a few categories: chat-based assistants, IDE agents, CLI agents, and project bootstrappers.

But the real leverage does not come from the interface.

It comes from two building blocks:

1. Skills and commands
2. Subagents

They help you start treating agents as programmable collaborators.

1️⃣ Skills and commands

A skill is a reusable, structured workflow encoded as a Markdown playbook. In Claude Code, these are just Markdown files in a .claude directory.

Instead of telling the agent, "Release this library,"

I give it a step-by-step procedure defined in one file.

Some examples I use daily:

- /release
- /init-library
- /create-github-repo
- /process

If I repeat a workflow twice, it becomes a command.

Over time, the agent stops being a chatbot and becomes an operator that follows my engineering standards.

2️⃣ Subagents

Agents have long but finite context windows. Over long sessions, performance degrades. I call this context rot.

Large transcripts, long articles, and big diffs pollute the context.

Subagents solve this. A subagent is a separate agent with a fresh context window.

I use this pattern heavily in my Telegram Writing Assistant.

--

posts.text:
Developer cheatsheet to turn a chatbot into a coding agent:

1) Chatbot vs agent decision

Decide upfront whether you actually need an agent. Agents are only worth it when you need actions like file I/O, code execution, or search.

2) Tool schema definition

Define concrete tools with strict schemas describing names, parameters, and constraints, and expose only what the agent should be allowed to do.

3) Tool execution loop

Implement a loop where the model proposes tool calls, your system executes them, and the results are fed back into the conversation state.

4) Project-scoped editing tools

Provide file and shell access scoped to a project root, with guardrails to prevent unsafe commands and accidental damage.

5) Project template scaffolding

Start each run from a clean template copied into a fresh directory so all agent edits remain isolated and reproducible.

6) System prompt as documentation

Use the system prompt to document the tech stack, file structure, and rules, and require the model to plan before acting.

Use this as a checklist when building a tool-using coding agent on top of your preferred stack and LLM API.

I needed a compact, persistent, local search library in Python.

I couldn't find one that met all my requirements.

So I built my own.

I just published the full workflow in my newsletter, where I cover:

- How I defined the requirements
- How I researched existing solutions with ChatGPT
- Why they didn't fit

The post isn't just about the library. It's about the process of going from a vague requirement to a working, published package.

I also share updates on:

- Our first offline meetup in Berlin
- An upcoming 1B-row data engineering workshop

posts.text:
Long-running agents have a context problem.

As they run, their prompts fill up with tool logs, stale diffs, repeated outputs, and irrelevant observations.

Eventually, the model starts missing important signals buried inside oversized prompts.

This is the "lost-in-the-middle" effect in practice.

In this upcoming webinar, Ivan Potapov and Tobias Lindenbauer will share research and practical insights on context engineering for agents.

We'll discuss:

- Masking vs summarization trade-offs
- Compressing bulky tool output
- Pruning dead branches in agent trajectories
- Reducing unnecessary LLM calls and cutting costs

Then we'll zoom out to bigger design questions:

How should memory hierarchies be structured?
How do standardized tool interfaces like MCP reduce context debt?
What does it mean to treat context engineering as something you train and iterate on, not just script?

Tobias recently presented work at NeurIPS 2025 on efficient context management strategies for code agents.

Ivan's recent work focuses on long-running agents, memory, retrieval, and why many code-first agent designs fail in production.

If you're building agents beyond toy demos, this discussion should be relevant.

Register here: https://luma.com/4298mc3j

- Produce mock event data into Redpanda

- Handling late and out-of-order data with watermarks and windows
- Configuring Flink checkpointing for resiliency
- Using the PyFlink Table API to write SQL-like transformations in Python

Why are entry-level data and software engineering roles so hard to get right now?

AI is not the...

posts.text:
Why are entry-level data and software engineering roles so hard to get right now?

AI is not the only reason, but it has changed hiring incentives.

1. Companies are under pressure

Slower markets, tighter budgets, fewer hires.

2. AI boosts senior productivity

One experienced engineer with AI tools can now do work that used to require a small team. From a company’s perspective, prompting AI is often cheaper than onboarding and managing juniors.

3. Hiring shifts as a result

Many teams prefer one strong engineer + AI over several junior roles. Entry-level openings shrink, competition explodes.

This does not mean learning data engineering, SQL, or software engineering is useless.

And AI doesn't replace skills. It raises expectations for how quickly you apply them.

For juniors, knowing the fundamentals is no longer enough on its own.

You're expected to:

🔸 Use AI to read and understand unfamiliar code
🔸 Iterate faster
🔸 Debug and reason about systems more efficiently

If you want to build these skills in practice, our Data Engineering Zoomcamp is free and open: https://github.com/DataTalksClub/data-engineering-zoomcamp

Free 25+ pages guide on building your own coding agent with Python, Jupyter, and Django

What it...

posts.text:
Free 25+ pages guide on building your own coding agent with Python, Jupyter, and Django

What it covers:

1. Decide: chatbot or agent

- Chatbot: text in -> text out
- Agent: loops with tool calls + stateful history

2. Define tool schemas

- Start with concrete functions: read_file, write_file, see_file_tree, execute_bash_command.
- Describe them using JSON schema (name, description, parameters).

3. Implement the tool loop

- Send messages + tools -> model.
- If it returns function_call, dispatch to Python.
- Append function_call + function_call_output back into the history.

4. Add project-editing tools

- Bind tools to a project_dir (sandbox).
- Block dangerous commands (e.g., runserver).
- Skip .venv, __pycache__, node_modules.

5. Scaffold a template repo

- Clone a minimal Django template.
- Copy it per project, then let the agent refactor and extend it.

6. Write a real system prompt

- Explain the stack, file tree, and constraints.
- Tell the model to plan first, then call tools to execute.

Get your free guide here: https://maven.com/p/f2d4cd/build-your-own-coding-agent-free-guide

posts.text:
Data Analyst vs. Data Engineer vs. Analytics Engineer: What's the Difference?

These roles often get mixed up, especially early in a data career.

Here's a practical way to think about them, based on how teams work:

1. Data Analysts

- Focus on what's happening in the data
- Build reports, dashboards, and analyses
- Translate numbers into insights
- Usually closest to business and product

2. Data Engineers

- Make data usable and reliable
- Build pipelines to ingest, clean, and store raw data
- Maintain data warehouses separate from production systems
- Enable analysts, data scientists, and ML engineers to do their work

3. Analytics Engineers

- Sit between analysis and engineering
- Turn raw data into clean, well-modeled tables
- Less infrastructure-heavy than data engineers
- Less business-facing than analysts
If you want to start or switch into data engineering, we offer a free, hands-on course: https://github.com/DataTalksClub/data-engineering-zoomcamp

posts.text:
I recently ran a workshop on building safe AI agents with guardrails.

One part of it focuses on building a search engine for a real FAQ before adding any agent logic.

The example uses a large FAQ for a Data Engineering course hosted on GitHub: 300+ questions, written by students.

We go through this step by step:

🔸 Fetch the FAQ data directly from GitHub
🔸 Parse questions and answers into a clean Python structure
🔸 Index the content to make it searchable
🔸 Verify that search returns relevant results

Only after that do we add an agent on top.

Retrieval and data grounding are important parts of an agent's design, because an agent is only as good as its access to data.

If retrieval is weak, the agent will confidently answer incorrectly.

My workshop shows how to ground an agent in real, verifiable data before adding guardrails and agentic behavior.

Here are the materials:

Video: https://youtu.be/Sk1aqwNJWT4?si=T6afVvKelro438OQ
Code: https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/workshops/tree/main/guardrails

This workshop is also a preview of the AI Engineering Buildcamp, where we go deeper into agent design, evaluation, monitoring, and guardrails as a system.

posts.text:
What are guardrails for AI agents?
Here's a simple way to think about them:

1. What are guardrails?

Guardrails are mechanisms that control how the model reacts to user input and what the user ultimately sees.

2. Why are guardrails important?

An agent will try to be helpful, even when it shouldn't.

For example, imagine an agent built to answer questions about a course.

Without guardrails:
🔸 A student can ask for pizza recipes
🔸 The agent will try to answer
🔸 You spend tokens and money on completely off-topic requests

Guardrails prevent this.

They let you define what is allowed and what is not, before or after the model responds.

3. In practice, guardrails help you:

🔸 Block off-topic questions early
🔸 Refuse requests you don't want to support
🔸 Avoid unsafe or inappropriate outputs
🔸 Save money by stopping useless calls

You decide what the agent is for. Guardrails enforce that decision.

Once agents are exposed to real users, guardrails stop being optional. They become part of the system design.

I walk through this step by step in a free workshop:

Video: https://youtu.be/Sk1aqwNJWT4?si=T6afVvKelro438OQ
Code: https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/workshops/tree/main/guardrails

We've just started the course, and you still have one buffer week to join and catch up.

posts.text:
When building agents, what is the difference between skills and commands?
They look similar, but they serve different roles.

1. Commands are explicit. You can think of them as user-driven shortcuts

🔸 The user knows exactly what should happen
🔸 The user triggers it directly, for example /kit
🔸 The agent simply executes the instruction

2. Skills are implicit

🔸 The user describes a task in natural language
🔸 The agent decides whether a skill applies
🔸 The agent loads and uses the skill autonomously

The user never says, "Use this skill"

Skills encode operational knowledge. They tell the agent how to do something, so it doesn't have to guess.

3. The key distinction is who makes the decision:

🔸 Commands: the user decides
🔸 Skills: the agent decides

Commands are best when the intent is precise.

posts.text:
10 examples of function calling in practice

Function calling lets LLMs connect with tools and take actions using these tools.

Quick distinction:

- Function is an implementation in your runtime (Python/JS/API).

- Tool is the contract you register for the LLM (name + typed schema + permissions). A tool is usually backed by one function, but it can orchestrate many.

1. Calendar & meetings

- Prompt: "Book 30 min with Alice tomorrow at 15:00."
- Tools: create_calendar_event(title, start, attendees)
- Effect: Event created; invite sent.

2. Docs & notes

- Prompt: "Summarize this PDF and save the notes to Notion."
- Tools: extract_text(file), create_notion_page(title, content)
- Effect: Summary page appears in your workspace.

3. CRM & sales ops

- Prompt: “Add this lead and enrich with company data.”
- Tools: create_crm_contact(data), enrich_with_clearbit(email)
- Effect: New contact with firmographics; owner assigned.

4. Support triage

- Prompt: “Route this ticket and draft a first reply.”
- Tools: classify_ticket(text), create_ticket(queue), draft_reply(context)
- Effect: Ticket filed to the right queue with a suggested response.

5. Data & reporting

- Prompt: “Revenue by region for the last 7 days—export to Sheets.”
- Tools: query_db(sql), create_google_sheet(name, rows)
- Effect: Fresh report in Google Sheets; link returned.

6. Files & automation

- Prompt: “Rename these images, compress, and upload to S3.”
- Tools: transform_images(params), upload_s3(bucket, paths)
- Effect: Optimized assets live in your bucket.

7. DevOps

- Prompt: “Is service X healthy? If not, roll back to the last stable.”
- Tools: get_status(service), rollback_deploy(service, version)
- Effect: Status reported; rollback executed if needed.

8. HR & recruiting

- Prompt: “Schedule a loop with three interviewers next week.”
- Tools: find_slots(attendees), create_calendar_event(series)
- Effect: Calendar holds with invites and meeting links.

9. Internal search + answer

- Prompt: “What’s our PTO policy?”
- Tools: semantic_search(kb, query), retrieve(doc_ids)
- Effect: Answer grounded in your knowledge base with citations.

10. Email & comms

- Prompt: “Send the weekly update to the team and attach the report.”
- Tools: generate_summary(data), send_email(to, subject, body, attachments)
- Effect: Email sent with the latest metrics and file.

Want to learn how to use function calling? I made a free guide on building your own AI coding agent with function calling and OpenAI API. You can get it here: https://maven.com/p/f2d4cd/build-your-own-coding-agent-free-guide

posts.text:
CSV files lack a schema.

When you load a CSV with Pandas, it must infer column types from the data, often leading to issues:

🔸 Integer columns become floats due to missing values
🔸 Datetime columns remain as strings
🔸 You receive warnings that are easy to overlook but challenging to debug later

In my Docker for Data Engineering workshop, I demonstrated a straightforward solution: explicitly define the schema.

Instead of relying on inference, provide a dtype mapping when reading the CSV:

🔸 IDs are read as integers
🔸 Timestamps are parsed as datetimes
🔸 Missing values are handled intentionally

This is crucial because type issues often arise much later:

🔸 When writing to a database
🔸 When switching from Pandas to Spark
🔸 When performing aggregations or joins

If you missed the workshop, here's the recording: https://www.youtube.com/live/lP8xXebHmuE?si=SrME-d1CtPqjnXGu

It will be used to update the Docker module in our free Data Engineering Zoomcamp course.

posts.text:
4 key components of AI agent architecture in its simplest form:

1. Brain: The LLM. It reasons, plans, and decides what to do next.

2. Instructions: The system prompt. It defines the agent's role, boundaries, and behavior.

3. Tools: Functions the agent can call to interact with the world:
reading files, writing code, running commands, searching data.

4. Memory: The conversation history and tool results that provide context across steps.

How this works together is what people call the agentic loop:

🔸 The user gives a task
🔸 The agent reasons based on instructions and memory
🔸 It decides to respond or call a tool
🔸 Tool results are added to memory
🔸 The loop continues until the task is complete

The agent decides when to stop.

Once you see this loop clearly, agent frameworks become much easier to reason about. They're mostly different ways of wiring these same components together.

If you want a hands-on walkthrough of this architecture, I've shared free workshop materials.

🔸 Video: https://youtu.be/OhgDEZfHsvg
🔸 Code: https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/workshops/tree/main/agent-skills

posts.text:
I tried Claude Code briefly about half a year ago and didn't like the terminal-first experience.

I preferred having an AI assistant directly in my IDE, so I stuck with Copilot.

But recently, Claude Code started popping up everywhere on social media, so I decided to give it another try.

One thing that caught my attention: Claude slash commands.

They're defined in an extremely simple way: you add a markdown file to .claude/commands and describe what the command should do.

Out of curiosity, I created two commands:

🔸 /kid: generates a random, often absurd project idea
🔸 /parent: implements it in HTML + JavaScript

Kid asks. Parent builds. Repeat.

I asked Claude to run this loop multiple times. It produced around 25 small projects:

🔸 Mostly single-file HTML (HTML + CSS + JS)
🔸 A few simple Python scripts
🔸 Zero external dependencies

Some examples: Invisible Pet Walker, Sneeze Simulator, Weird Plants Garden, Silly Symphony (Web Audio), Robot Chef inventing bizarre dishes.

You can open them directly in a browser. I published them via GitHub Pages.

You can check these projects here: https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/claude-code-kid-parent

Read more about how I tried to run Claude Code forever, why it kept stopping, and how the Ralph Wiggum plugin (almost) solved it in my latest newsletter: https://alexeyondata.substack.com/p/my-experiments-with-claude-code

posts.text:
4 key components of AI agent architecture in its simplest form:

1. Brain: The LLM. It reasons, plans, and decides what to do next.

2. Instructions: The system prompt. It defines the agent's role, boundaries, and behavior.

3. Tools: Functions the agent can call to interact with the world:
reading files, writing code, running commands, searching data.

4. Memory: The conversation history and tool results that provide context across steps.

How this works together is what people call the agentic loop:

🔸 The user gives a task
🔸 The agent reasons based on instructions and memory
🔸 It decides to respond or call a tool
🔸 Tool results are added to memory
🔸 The loop continues until the task is complete

The agent decides when to stop.

Once you see this loop clearly, agent frameworks become much easier to reason about. They're mostly different ways of wiring these same components together.

If you want a hands-on walkthrough of this architecture, I've shared free workshop materials.

🔸 Video: https://youtu.be/OhgDEZfHsvg

posts.text:
I recently ran a workshop on building safe AI agents with guardrails.

One part of it focuses on building a search engine for a real FAQ before adding any agent logic.

The example uses a large Data Engineering course FAQ stored on GitHub.
300+ questions, written by real students.

We go through this step by step:

🔸 Fetch the FAQ data directly from GitHub
🔸 Parse questions and answers into a clean Python structure
🔸 Index the content to make it searchable
🔸 Verify that search returns relevant results

Only after that do we add an agent on top.

Retrieval and data grounding are important parts of an agent's design, because an agent is only as good as its access to data.

If retrieval is weak, the agent will confidently answer incorrectly.

My workshop shows how to ground an agent in real, verifiable data before adding guardrails and agentic behavior.

Here's an example from a recent workshop where I built an FAQ assistant that answers student questions based on an FAQ document.

We start with a simple Python search function that queries an indexed FAQ.

The key step is turning that function into a tool and giving it to an agent.

Here's how to do it:

🔸 Define a search function over the FAQ index
🔸 Decorate it as a tool so the agent can call it
🔸 Create an agent with clear system instructions
🔸 Assign the tool to the agent

In my case, instructions tell the agent:

🔸 You are a teaching assistant
🔸 Your job is to answer questions using the FAQ
🔸 Use the search tool when needed

When a user asks a question, the agent:

🔸 Decides whether to call the tool
🔸 Generates a search query
🔸 Inspects the returned results
🔸 Produces the final answer

You can inspect every tool call to see exactly how the agent reasons and why it chose a particular answer.

This material comes from a free workshop on building safe AI agents, where we go from search to agents and then add guardrails on top.

Materials:

Video: https://youtu.be/Sk1aqwNJWT4?si=T6afVvKelro438OQ
Code: https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/workshops/tree/main/guardrails

posts.text:
What are guardrails for AI agents?
Here's a simple way to think about them:

1. What are guardrails?

Guardrails are mechanisms that control how the model reacts to user input and what the user ultimately sees.

2. Why are guardrails important?

An agent will try to be helpful, even when it shouldn't.

For example, imagine an agent built to answer questions about a course.

Without guardrails:
🔸 A student can ask for pizza recipes
🔸 The agent will try to answer
🔸 You spend tokens and money on completely off-topic requests

Guardrails prevent this.

They let you define what is allowed and what is not, before or after the model responds.

3. In practice, guardrails help you:

🔸 Block off-topic questions early
🔸 Refuse requests you don't want to support
🔸 Avoid unsafe or inappropriate outputs
🔸 Save money by stopping useless calls

You decide what the agent is for. Guardrails enforce that decision.

Once agents are exposed to real users, guardrails stop being optional. They become part of the system design.

I walk through this step by step in a free workshop:

Video: https://youtu.be/Sk1aqwNJWT4?si=T6afVvKelro438OQ
Code: https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/workshops/tree/main/guardrails

posts.text:
Why are entry-level data and software engineering roles so hard to get right now?

AI is not the only reason, but it has changed hiring incentives.

1. Companies are under pressure

Slower markets, tighter budgets, fewer hires.

2. AI boosts senior productivity

One experienced engineer with AI tools can now do work that used to require a small team. From a company’s perspective, prompting AI is often cheaper than onboarding and managing juniors.

3. Hiring shifts as a result

Many teams prefer one strong engineer + AI over several junior roles. Entry-level openings shrink, competition explodes.

This does not mean learning data engineering, SQL, or software engineering is useless.

And AI doesn't replace skills. It raises expectations for how quickly you apply them.

For juniors, knowing the fundamentals is no longer enough on its own.

You're expected to:

🔸 Use AI to read and understand unfamiliar code
🔸 Iterate faster
🔸 Debug and reason about systems more efficiently

If you want to build these skills in practice, our Data Engineering Zoomcamp is free and open: https://github.com/DataTalksClub/data-engineering-zoomcamp

posts.text:
I enjoy working with AI agents right from my phone.
If you read my newsletter, you've likely already seen some of my workflows.

Usually, I rely on GitHub Copilot.

This time, I decided to test a different setup using Claude Code.

I asked an agent to:

🔸 Create the most cost-effective AWS instance with 8 GB of RAM
🔸 Install Claude Code and reuse my existing configuration
🔸 Expose everything via a web interface

It worked.

The agent provisioned an EC2 instance, installed dependencies, and set up:

🔸 a web UI
🔸 a browser-based terminal

Now, I have a dedicated remote environment I can fully control from my phone.

I can send instructions.
It runs independently.
No laptop needed.

Some trade-offs, honestly:

🔸 Less seamless than Copilot
🔸 More setup required
🔸 More control
🔸 Less friction than managing infrastructure manually

I share experiments and results like that in my newsletter: https://alexeyondata.substack.com/

posts.text:
When building agents, what is the difference between skills and commands?
They look similar, but they serve different roles.

1. Commands are explicit. You can think of them as user-driven shortcuts

🔸 The user knows exactly what should happen
🔸 The user triggers it directly, for example /kit
🔸 The agent simply executes the instruction

2. Skills are implicit

🔸 The user describes a task in natural language
🔸 The agent decides whether a skill applies
🔸 The agent loads and uses the skill autonomously

The user never says, "Use this skill"

Skills encode operational knowledge. They tell the agent how to do something, so it doesn't have to guess.

3. The key distinction is who makes the decision:

🔸 Commands: the user decides
🔸 Skills: the agent decides

Commands are best when the intent is precise.

Skills are better when you want reusable, predictable agent behavior across tasks and projects.

If you want to go deeper, I've shared a free workshop on implementing skills from scratch:

🔸 Video: https://youtu.be/OhgDEZfHsvg
🔸 Code: https://github.com/alexeygrigorev/workshops/tree/main/agent-skills

I also teach how to build production-ready AI agents in my AI Engineering Buildcamp. We go deeper into agent design, evaluation, monitoring, and guardrails as a system.

We've just started the course, and you still have one buffer week to join and catch up.

posts.text:
I recently ran a two-day, in-person workshop on AI agents with the data team at NOW GmbH in Berlin.

Day 1 was about fundamentals.

We built everything bottom-up, directly in code:

🔸 LLMs and the OpenAI API
🔸 Alternatives to OpenAI: Groq, Anthropic, Bedrock, Gemini
🔸 RAG with text, vector, and hybrid search
🔸 Agentic RAG patterns where the model decides when and what to search
🔸 Tool calling, agent loops, and MCP
🔸 Using PydanticAI to orchestrate agents

Day 2 was fully focused on building.

We implemented a custom coding agent from scratch:

🔸 Set up a Django project template as the agent's working environment
🔸 Implemented tools for reading files, writing code, running commands, and navigating the project
🔸 Built a coding agent step by step, first with ToyAIKit to understand the mechanics, then with PydanticAI for production-ready features
🔸 Explored multi-agent patterns such as planner-executor and coordinator agents
🔸 Added monitoring with Pydantic Logfire
🔸 Introduced guardrails: input validation, output checks, and execution limits

The group was highly engaged, asked great questions, and worked through the exercises together.

Thanks to the NOW GmbH team for two focused and productive days!

posts.text:
We recently ran a workshop on fact-checking with Wikidata.

We showed LLMs' knowledge cutoff by asking a simple question: "Who is the current president?"

And the model confidently hallucinated.

We used Wikidata MCP to retrieve structured facts fetched directly from Wikidata. The system we built evaluated whether a claim was true or false.

In the second part of the workshop, Philippe Saadé, our guest speaker, showed a fact-checking pipeline you can adapt to real projects:

🔸 One small model to rerank and select relevant Wikidata facts
🔸 Pne small model to verify the claim against those facts

If you're interested in grounding LLMs in real, verifiable data, this was a very solid example of how to do it.

You can watch the workshop recording here: https://www.youtube.com/live/eT_VTTeaig4?si=7femIRxHrmzDffkw

posts.text:
What are skills in AI agents?

In one of the workshops, I demo a GitHub Fetch skill.

The task seems simple: retrieve files from a GitHub repository. But without this skill, the agent must guess how to:

- Interact with GitHub
- Choose the right commands
- Navigate the repository structure

A skill provides a reusable set of instructions that guides the agent through tasks step by step.

Specifically, the GitHub Fetch skill instructs the agent on:

- Using the gh CLI
- Listing repository contents
- Navigating directories
- Downloading specific files

With these validated instructions, skills minimize reasoning errors by encoding operational knowledge.

In the demo, we used this skill to fetch two commands from a GitHub repo:

- /kid generates a wild project idea
- /parent implements it as code

These commands are stored in GitHub, and the agent uses the GitHub Fetch skill to automatically retrieve them.

Skills offer benefits like:

- Making behavior predictable
- Avoiding repeated prompts
- Reusing hard-won instructions
- Scaling beyond one-off demos

I teach how to build production-ready AI agents in my AI Bootcamp. We go deeper into agent design, evaluation, monitoring, and guardrails as a system.

The next cohort starts tomorrow: https://maven.com/alexey-grigorev/from-rag-to-agents

posts.text:
I'm restructuring the AI Engineering Buildcamp curriculum.

Some of the AI Engineering Buildcamp course participants from the first cohort shared this feedback with me:

"The content is extremely dense and valuable, but the pace felt too fast."

For people with full-time jobs, there wasn't always enough time to pause, process, and practice. At the same time, some learners wanted more depth, more tools, more comparisons.

That's why I decided to redesign the course to make it more focused.

That way:

🔸 Busy professionals can focus on what matters
🔸 Those who want to go deeper still have room to explore

I recently ran a workshop on guardrails for AI agents.

The goal was to make agents safer and more predictable in real-world use.

We started by building a small FAQ assistant, then added guardrails on top:

🔸 Input guardrails to block irrelevant or unsafe requests before the agent runs
🔸 Output guardrails to prevent inappropriate promises, policy violations, or leakage

We also covered how to:

🔸 Cancel agent execution early when a guardrail trips
🔸 Run guardrails in parallel to avoid extra latency
🔸 Enforce boundaries like academic integrity and scope limits

What happens if you ask Claude Code to run slash commands forever?

posts.text:
What happens if you ask Claude Code to run slash commands forever?

I created two Claude Code commands:

🔸 /kid: generates a random, often absurd project idea
🔸 /parent: implements it in HTML + JavaScript

I wanted Claude Code to repeat the following process automatically:

1. Run /kid to generate a new idea
2. Run /parent to implement that idea
3. Go back to step 1 and repeat

But Claude kept pausing. I had to nudge it manually each time.

Seeking a hands-off solution, I explored stop hooks, but they were outdated and failed. Then, I found the Ralph Wiggum plugin.

It prompts Claude to continue with the next step when Claude finishes a task and stops.

I tested this on a small project (a metabolism simulator). On Windows, it didn't fully work because the plugin is implemented as a Bash command. From what I can tell, it should work on macOS or Linux.

Discover more on my Claude Code journey and my own version of the Ralph Wiggum plugin in my latest newsletter: https://alexeyondata.substack.com/p/my-experiments-with-claude-code

posts.text:
Learning in public is often underestimated.

In practice, it changes both how you learn and what opportunities come your way.

Here are 8 benefits of learning in public:

1. Your work becomes discoverable: When you share progress publicly, recruiters, employers, or collaborators can find your work without you actively reaching out.

2. You understand topics more deeply: Explaining what you learn forces you to structure your thinking, notice gaps, and clarify concepts.

3. You get earlier feedback: Public posts invite comments from people working on similar problems, helping you catch mistakes and learn alternative approaches.

4. You build a visible track record: Regular sharing creates a history of work that signals consistency and competence over time.

5. It adds accountability: Knowing others can see your progress makes it easier to stay consistent and finish long or difficult learning goals.

6. You get help when you are stuck: Sharing difficulties publicly increases the chance that someone can unblock you, instead of struggling in isolation.

7. You create concrete proof of skills: Posts, code, and small projects give others something tangible to evaluate, not just claims on a CV.

8. Unexpected opportunities emerge: Public learning can lead to collaborations, speaking invites, or side projects that are unlikely to happen through private learning alone.
If you want to learn more about the practice of learning in public, read my recent newsletter edition: https://alexeyondata.substack.com/p/benefits-of-learning-in-public-and

A common question I receive is: Should I take the Data Engineering Zoomcamp? Do I know enough, or should I upskill first?

My advice is straightforward: use the Docker workshop as a diagnostic test.

I recently conducted a Docker workshop, which will replace the Docker section of the course. It will eventually become the first module, but you can access it now.

If you have time and plan to take the course, start with this workshop.

The aim is to pinpoint your knowledge gaps.

As you progress through it, consider these questions:

🔸 Is using the command line challenging?
🔸 Do you feel lost when something breaks?
🔸 Are the basic concepts unfamiliar to you?

If you answer yes to any of these, it's a valuable signal.

You have time before the course starts, and this highlights exactly what you need to practice:

If the command line is difficult, practice working in the terminal. Or if Python is a weakness, focus on improving your Python fundamentals.

The Docker workshop helps you identify areas to work on.

posts.text:
Guardrails are critical for AI agents

With AI agents that take actions, failures become real risks

Without guardrails, agents can:

🔶 Call the wrong tools
🔶 Let users misuse your product
🔶 Ignore hard constraints
🔶 Leak sensitive data
🔶 Fail silently while looking “successful”
🔶 Damage your company’s reputation

Prompts alone don’t solve this. We need a way to check whether the inputs and outputs of our agents conform to the standards we define.

That’s where guardrails come in. Tomorrow, we’ll learn how to add safety checks to your agents.

You’ll learn how to:

🔶 Build a working agent from scratch
🔶 Understand where guardrails actually sit
🔶 Apply production-ready input, tool, and output guardrails
🔶 Use a reusable mental model across agents and frameworks

If you’re moving from demos to production, this is a must.

Sign up here: https://maven.com/p/569db8/building-safe-ai-agents-with-guardrails

AI agents are moving beyond single-shot prompts and ad-hoc customization.

They shift toward modular, reusable procedural knowledge, now called agent skills.

posts.text:
Docker containers are stateless by default.

Anything you create inside a container (files, data, outputs) disappears as soon as the container stops.

So how do we work with code and data?

The answer: volume mapping.

In Docker, you can mount a directory from your local machine into the container.

This way:

🔸 Your files live on your laptop
🔸 The container can read and modify them
🔸 Restarting or deleting the container doesn't delete your work

You run code in an isolated environment, but the data persists outside of it.

Using volume mapping is part of my Docker for Data Engineering workshop.

Watch it here: https://www.youtube.com/live/lP8xXebHmuE?si=SrME-d1CtPqjnXGu

The recording is now part of the Data Engineering Zoomcamp, which starts on January 12, 2026.

Join the course to learn Docker the way it's used in real data projects: https://github.com/DataTalksClub/data-engineering-zoomcamp

posts.text:
The job market is tough right now, especially for entry-level roles.

Companies can often get the productivity of several junior engineers from one experienced hire.

That means more competition and higher expectations.

So the question I hear most often is: How do I stand out?

My answer is very practical: Don't build generic projects. Build domain-specific ones.

Here's the strategy I recommend:

1. Start by looking at open positions on LinkedIn. Try to understand which domains companies work in: e-commerce, finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and so on. Pick a domain you’re actually interested in.

2. Then do some research:

🔸 read tech blogs from companies hiring in that domain
🔸 look at the kinds of data problems they describe
🔸 streaming systems, event processing, analytics pipelines, etc.

3. Next step: replicate those problems on a smaller scale.

If you can find a similar dataset, use it. If not, generate one.

Then try to solve the same type of problem, just simplified.

This does a few important things:

🔸 you understand what problems exist in that domain
🔸 you already get exposure before being hired
🔸 you stand out from candidates who only have generic projects

4. You can mention this work in your cover letter.

You can talk about it during interviews.

When they ask questions, you have something concrete and relevant to discuss.

Do this for a couple of projects, and that's usually enough to make a difference.

5. This is also why, in my courses, we focus not just on foundations, but on projects.

With this approach, you can already build one strong project for your portfolio, start applying, and continue adding more over time.

We're launching Data Engineering Zoomcamp 2026 on January 12, 2026.

Register here: https://github.com/DataTalksClub/data-engineering-zoomcamp

LLMs can sound very confident even when they're outputting wrong facts.

As soon as you ask LLMs about concrete entities or relationships they weren't trained on, hallucinations become a problem.

In these cases, prompting alone doesn't fix the issue. You need ground truth that the model can query and verify.

Philippe Saadé will focus on this topic at the upcoming DataTalksClub workshop.

He'll show how to use Wikidata, accessed via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), as a structured and verifiable source of knowledge for LLM-based systems.

Time: 4:30 PM CET

We'll cover:

🔸 Using Wikidata for factual verification
🔸 Querying Wikidata through MCP
🔸 Combining MCP with an LLM to verify claims
🔸 Designing evidence-based pipelines instead of relying on model memory
🔸 Semantic search over Wikidata statements
🔸 Reranking evidence with an LLM
🔸 Verifying claims using an NLI model

payload.preview: In a recent session, I showed how to turn a scraping workflow into something durable and...

posts.text:
In a recent session, I showed how to turn a scraping workflow into something durable and recoverable using Temporal.

When you're building systems that depend on the network, failures are inevitable.

Proxies break, connections drop, and external services behave unpredictably.

If the code can't recover, execution stops.

That's why durability matters for long-running workflows. When something breaks, the system should be able to retry automatically and continue execution.

Before introducing Temporal, I first cleaned up the code.

The original implementation lives in a Jupyter notebook, so I convert it into a Python script, move imports and configuration to the top, and separate responsibilities like proxy setup, video discovery, and processing logic. The goal is to turn messy exploratory code into something that can become a proper workflow.

Once this code runs as a Temporal workflow, the behavior changes. Execution continues even when failures happen. Retries are handled automatically. The workflow becomes durable, recoverable, and reliable by design.

This is the difference between code that usually works and systems that are built to survive failure.

If you're working on scraping pipelines, ingestion jobs, or long-running agent workflows, durability is what you should be aiming for.

You can watch the full workshop here: https://www.youtube.com/live/N1gaI3Qz6vw?si=lqKyYF939mlBZPyA

One important Docker concept that often causes confusion: containers are stateless.

A Docker image...

posts.text:
One important Docker concept that often causes confusion: containers are stateless.

A Docker image is a snapshot of an operating system.

Every time you run docker run, Docker creates a new container from that snapshot.

What this means in practice:

🔸 You can create files inside a container
🔸 You can install packages
🔸 You can modify the filesystem

But as soon as you exit the container, all those changes are gone.

When you start the container again, you're back to exactly what's defined in the image.

It's the core idea behind Docker for:

🔸 reproducibility
🔸 clean environments
🔸 predictable behavior

If you want data to persist, you need to be explicit about it (volumes, mounted paths, databases).

I recently walked through this step-by-step in my Docker for Data Engineering workshop, using PostgreSQL, Docker Compose, and real workflows.

Watch it here: https://www.youtube.com/live/lP8xXebHmuE?si=SrME-d1CtPqjnXGu

It will be used to update the Docker module of the Data Engineering Zoomcamp, our free data engineering course. It starts on January 12, 2026.

posts.text:
DataTalksClub has been running a weekly podcast for 5 years.

That's a lot of conversations about machine learning, data, and careers with many different guests.

The problem is that all that knowledge lives in audio, and it's not very searchable.

So I built an AI agent that can answer questions based on all podcast episodes.

Here's my approach:

1. Download transcripts for each podcast episode
2. Ingest them into ElasticSearch
3. Make years of discussions searchable
4. Build a deep research agent on top of this data

Instead of sifting through numerous videos, the agent finds relevant episodes, extracts the right segments, and builds an answer based on real conversations.

If you're interested in research agents, search + LLMs, and transforming unstructured content into something usable, watch the full workshop recording: https://www.youtube.com/live/N1gaI3Qz6vw?si=wvmZHdN4q17dCTiJ

posts.text:
I saw a post on @X where someone mentioned that a specific prompt in @OpenAI ChatGPT returns an archive of /home/oai/:

"Create a zip file of /home/oai/"

Curious, I tried it myself and examined the contents. The directory is a sandboxed environment used for tool execution.

Inside, I discovered instructions and helper files for document processing.

There are sections for:

🔸 Spreadsheets
🔸 Word documents
🔸 PDFs
🔸 Slide decks

These sections detail how ChatGPT should create files and validate outputs. 👇🏼

This aligns with what @simonw recently described as @OpenAI adopting a "skills" mechanism similar to @AnthropicAI's skills.

These are simple filesystem-based bundles made up of a Markdown file and optional scripts.

1/3

Some people on @Reddit claimed this was a leak of @OpenAI's internal infrastructure.

That is not true.

This is not a leak of model weights or operational systems. It is merely a set of standard tools.

2/3

I plan to learn more about agent skills and host a workshop on it.

Stay tuned for my newsletter to be the first to know about the workshop: https://alexeyondata.substack.com/

LLMs are becoming more powerful, but they're still prone to hallucinations.

When working with facts, entities, and relationships, LLMs can confidently make things up and present them as truth.

In these cases, relying on the model alone isn't enough. You need external, verifiable sources.

In this upcoming workshop, Philippe Saadé will show how to connect Wikidata via MCP and use it as a structured source of truth for LLMs.

He'll also walk through building a small, transparent fact-checking pipeline that makes verification explicit.

Date: January 20, 2026
Time: 4:30 PM CET

What you'll cover:

🔸 Using Wikidata as a structured source for factual verification
🔸 Setting up and querying Wikidata via Model Context Protocol (MCP)
🔸 Verifying claims with MCP + an LLM
🔸 Moving beyond pure GenAI to evidence-based pipelines
🔸 Semantic search over Wikidata statements
🔸 LLM-based reranking of candidate evidence
🔸 Claim verification with an NLI model

Register here: https://luma.com/7fs5v7os

posts.text:
We frequently receive questions about the Data Engineering Zoomcamp.

Here are 5 main Q&As + how you can ask me your questions live:

1. How much time per week should I allocate to stay on track?

Estimated weekly workload based on homework statistics: approximately 10 hours per week. Beginners might need closer to 15-20 hours, especially for Module 1 (Docker), which is the most challenging.

2. What should I prepare before the course begins?

Key prerequisites:

- Install Docker early, especially if you're on Windows
- Create a GitHub account
- Join Slack
- Set up GCP
- Have a basic understanding of Python and SQL

3. Can I land a data engineering job after the Zoomcamp?

Yes, many do!

The course teaches the key 20% of skills for 80% of real-world tasks.

You'll need a strong project and some self-study, but it's a great start for junior or mid-level roles.

4. Is the course suitable for beginners or recent graduates?

It depends.

Comfort with basic programming and the terminal is needed.
SQL and Python basics are a must.

Aspiring data engineers can start here.
For general software roles, it might be wise to wait.

5. What's new in this cohort?

The Docker module is updated. It now guides you through a full workflow with Docker, PostgreSQL, pgAdmin, and Docker Compose. Learn to run and link multiple services effortlessly.

Want to ask your question and get an answer from me? Join me for a live Q&A on Monday, December 15.

I'm hosting a new workshop on building a deep-research YouTube agent.

This time, I'm putting a major focus on something most tutorials skip: the data ingestion pipeline.

Why? Because this is the most subtle and failure-prone part of the whole system.

1/5

Transcripts disappear, rate limits hit, proxies break… and if your ingestion isn't durable, your agent won't survive in production.

Many tutorials ignore this step entirely: the resulting agents look nice in demos but unusable in real workflows.

2/5

🔹 Transform an unreliable script into a robust Temporal workflow
🔹 Implement retries, proxy rotation, error handling
🔹 Index transcripts in Elasticsearch for fast searches
🔹 Develop a deep-research agent with PydanticAI
🔹 Ensure durability and observability via Temporal

3/5

By the end, you'll have a full pattern for building a Q&A system for any YouTube channel or internal video library.

4/5

This time, I'm putting a major focus on something most tutorials skip: the data ingestion pipeline.

posts.text:
3 parts of the MCP architecture: host, client, and server

🧵

1. MCP Host: the environment where your AI operates.

This could be your Claude UI, VS Code with Copilot, or Cursor—essentially any interface that can coordinate LLM actions.

2. MCP Client: the code that mediates between the host and the server.

It sends requests, receives responses, and manages communication according to the MCP standard.

3. MCP Server: the bridge to real-world data and tools.

Servers expose your files, Git repositories, Slack messages, or other applications through standardized connectors. Each tool (for example, a Slack MCP server) implements its own logic behind a consistent API.

4. This setup lets developers create LLM integrations that are:

🔸 Predictable: Uniform communication between clients and servers
🔸 Portable: Connects to various tools without altering code
🔸 Debuggable: Uses JSON so you can inspect every request and response

This explanation is based on Bhavani Ravi's workshop on MCP, where she explained how it connects LLMs with real-world tools, data systems, and developer workflows.

If you'd like to watch the full session, you can find the recording here: https://youtube.com/live/0IhZdcjddo4

posts.text:
MCP is built on key components known as primitives.

These define how clients and servers communicate, share data, and perform actions through a common language.

MCP servers introduce three main primitives:

1. Tools ➡️ Actions that perform tasks

Examples include generating a summary or fetching the weather. Each tool represents an operation the AI can activate.

2. Resources ➡️ Information sources

They don't perform actions but return data—such as files, configuration details, or other structured content that the AI can utilize.

3. Prompts ➡️ Text-generating functions

These return a string, often a reusable prompt template or instruction for the model.

This overview is based on Bhavani Ravi’s workshop on MCP, where she explained how it connects LLMs with real-world tools, data systems, and developer workflows.

MCP is built on key components known as primitives.

These define how clients and servers communicate, share data, and perform actions through a common language.

MCP servers introduce three main primitives:

1. Tools ➡️ Actions that perform tasks

Examples include generating a summary or fetching the weather. Each tool represents an operation the AI can activate.

2. Resources ➡️ Information sources

They don't perform actions but return data—such as files, configuration details, or other structured content that the AI can utilize.

3. Prompts ➡️ Text-generating functions

These return a string, often a reusable prompt template or instruction for the model.

posts.text:
We've reached the midterm projects at ML Zoomcamp!

Now, it's time to transition from notebooks to real, deployable machine learning applications.

Here's a quick list of 6 key tips for a successful submission:

1️⃣ Choose your problem wisely

Pick a project you're passionate about: something intriguing enough to keep you engaged in debugging and refining for two weeks.

2️⃣ Frame it clearly

Explain what you're predicting, why it matters, and how you'll measure success (e.g., accuracy, AUC, RMSE).

3️⃣ Keep data handling clean

Document your data sources, check for quality, and ensure your preprocessing steps are reproducible.

4️⃣ Model smartly

Begin with a baseline model, test at least three models, use cross-validation, and avoid data leakage.

5️⃣ Package it properly

Transition from notebook ➡️ scripts ➡️ web service ➡️ Docker.

A functional POST /predict endpoint and a Dockerfile are required.

6️⃣ Bonus points

Deploy to the cloud, document everything, and share your progress publicly.

💡 Pro tip: Clone your repo fresh before submission.

If it runs smoothly for you, it will run smoothly for reviewers.

Good luck, and remember: Deployment always takes longer than you expect so start early!

Submit your project here: https://courses.datatalks.club/ml-zoomcamp-2025/project/midterm

posts.text:
Setting up transfer learning? Your first big challenge is data prep, and not all frameworks handle it the same way.

With PyTorch, you get the granularity you need to:

🔸 Iterating through files and directories
🔸 Opening and reading images
🔸 Applying transformations (normalization, resizing, augmentation)

This level of control is perfect for intricate or custom data setups, but it requires more coding and debugging.

Conversely, Keras provides high-level utilities that automate iteration, batching, and transformations. This is ideal for quick experimentation.

So choose your framework based on your needs.

If you're interested in learning both tools, check out the 8th module of our free ML Zoomcamp: https://github.com/DataTalksClub/machine-learning-zoomcamp/tree/master/08-deep-learning

posts.text:
Why choose PyTorch over Keras for deep learning in 2025?

Keras still holds its ground.

It's fantastic for education, prototyping, and TensorFlow-native environments.

But for most modern deep learning workloads, PyTorch leads in industry adoption.

Here's why:

1. Most modern deep learning libraries are built PyTorch-first. You'll find faster updates, better documentation, and more active communities.

2. Almost every new deep learning paper, model, or open-source repo is released in PyTorch.

3. Dynamic computation graphs, native Python control flow, and easy debugging make PyTorch ideal for experimentation and custom architectures.

4. Distributed training, mixed precision, quantization, and production runtimes (like TorchServe or Triton) are well-integrated and mature.

5. From startups to Big Tech, PyTorch is the default stack across computer vision, NLP, multimodal models, and even edge deployment.

What's your experience with PyTorch vs. Keras?

If you want to learn how to use PyTorch, watch my live workshop on using PyTorch to train an image classifier: https://www.youtube.com/live/Ne25VujHRLA?si=NJffwngOMlFh6rGg
