posts.text:
During one of the workshops, I was asked: When do you actually need Kubernetes? And when is Docker alone enough?

It's a great question and one that comes up often.

Here's how I usually explain it 👇

1️⃣ Docker: the starting point

Docker is fantastic for packaging your app. If it works in Docker locally, it'll work in production—on Kubernetes, ECS, or any other container system.

But here’s the thing: In production, you never just "run Docker." You need something to:

🔸 Restart containers if they fail
🔸 Monitor health and performance
🔸 Collect logs and metrics

That's where we need container management systems.

2️⃣ Kubernetes (and ECS): managing at scale

Kubernetes is the industry standard for container orchestration.
It automates deployment, scaling, and recovery, ideal when you have multiple services or teams.

But it can be overkill for smaller setups.

3️⃣ The takeaway

🔸 Start with Docker to package and test your app.
🔸 Add a management layer like ECS when you need resilience and monitoring.
🔸 Move to Kubernetes only when your system's complexity truly requires it.

posts.text:
When deploying machine learning models, a common challenge is the reliance on a specific framework.

A model trained in TensorFlow or PyTorch might not run easily in another environment.

That's where ONNX can help.

1️⃣ What is ONNX?

ONNX is a model-agnostic format that allows you to convert models from various frameworks (like TensorFlow, Keras, PyTorch, and more) into a single, standardized format.

Once converted, the model can be deployed anywhere.

2️⃣ Why ONNX matters for deployment:

1. Freedom: Use any library, not bound by training choice
2. Swift Inference: Use optimized runtimes like ONNX for speed
3. Flexibility: Deploy on any hardware or environment
4. Integration: Mixed frameworks? No problem. Collaborate easily

3️⃣ In practice, this means you can:

✅ Train your model in PyTorch
✅ Export it to ONNX
✅ Run inference efficiently in production

4️⃣ ONNX bridges the gap between model training and production deployment, making ML systems more portable and maintainable.

If you're building deployable ML pipelines, learning ONNX is a small investment with huge returns.

Most AI chatbots can only talk. Function calling lets them connect with tools and take actions using these tools.

This is what an agent can do compared to a simple chatbot:

🔸 Access live data via API or other sources
🔸 Update data on your computer/other connected device
🔸 Do anything you can implement using code

Instead of just replying with text, the LLM can now propose a specific action like “create a calendar event” or “fetch today’s weather”

Here is how it works:

1. You define the tools (functions) the model is allowed to use.
2. The model decides to call one, passing arguments in a structured format.
3. Your system validates, executes, and returns the result for the conversation to continue.

This process is known as “function calling.” Without this, the model is limited to what it “knows” from training and the prompt.

I made a free guide on building your own AI coding agent with function calling and OpenAI API. You can get it here: https://maven.com/p/f2d4cd/build-your-own-coding-agent-free-guide

Aren't AI agents just fancy chatbots?

No, here’s the difference 👇

Most chatbots can only respond with text.
Agents can take action using tools.

With function calling, an agent can:

🔸 Fetch live data via APIs
🔸 Update files or data on your computer
🔸 Run any action you can implement in code

So instead of replying, “The meeting is tomorrow at 10”, the agent can actually create the calendar event for you.

How does it work?

1. You define the tools (functions) the model can use
2. The model decides when to call one, with structured arguments
3. Your system validates, executes, and passes results back into the conversation

That’s what makes it “agentic.” Without this, an LLM is limited to just its training data and your prompt.

I wrote a free step-by-step guide on how to build your own coding agent using function calling and the OpenAI API.

Download it here: https://maven.com/p/f2d4cd/build-your-own-coding-agent-free-guide

posts.text:
10 examples of function calling in practice

Function calling lets LLMs connect with tools and take actions using these tools.

Quick distinction:

- Function is an implementation in your runtime (Python/JS/API).

- Tool is the contract you register for the LLM (name + typed schema + permissions). A tool is usually backed by one function, but it can orchestrate many.

1. Calendar & meetings

- Prompt: "Book 30 min with Alice tomorrow at 15:00."
- Tools: create_calendar_event(title, start, attendees)
- Effect: Event created; invite sent.

2. Docs & notes

- Prompt: "Summarize this PDF and save the notes to Notion."
- Tools: extract_text(file), create_notion_page(title, content)
- Effect: Summary page appears in your workspace.

3. CRM & sales ops

- Prompt: “Add this lead and enrich with company data.”
- Tools: create_crm_contact(data), enrich_with_clearbit(email)
- Effect: New contact with firmographics; owner assigned.

4. Support triage

- Prompt: “Route this ticket and draft a first reply.”
- Tools: classify_ticket(text), create_ticket(queue), draft_reply(context)
- Effect: Ticket filed to the right queue with a suggested response.

5. Data & reporting

- Prompt: “Revenue by region for the last 7 days—export to Sheets.”
- Tools: query_db(sql), create_google_sheet(name, rows)
- Effect: Fresh report in Google Sheets; link returned.

6. Files & automation

- Prompt: “Rename these images, compress, and upload to S3.”
- Tools: transform_images(params), upload_s3(bucket, paths)
- Effect: Optimized assets live in your bucket.

7. DevOps

- Prompt: “Is service X healthy? If not, roll back to the last stable.”
- Tools: get_status(service), rollback_deploy(service, version)
- Effect: Status reported; rollback executed if needed.

8. HR & recruiting

- Prompt: “Schedule a loop with three interviewers next week.”
- Tools: find_slots(attendees), create_calendar_event(series)
- Effect: Calendar holds with invites and meeting links.

9. Internal search + answer

- Prompt: “What’s our PTO policy?”
- Tools: semantic_search(kb, query), retrieve(doc_ids)
- Effect: Answer grounded in your knowledge base with citations.

10. Email & comms

- Prompt: “Send the weekly update to the team and attach the report.”
- Tools: generate_summary(data), send_email(to, subject, body, attachments)
- Effect: Email sent with the latest metrics and file.

Want to learn how to use function calling? I made a free guide on building your own AI coding agent with function calling and OpenAI API. You can get it here: https://maven.com/p/f2d4cd/build-your-own-coding-agent-free-guide

Excited to share something new from the LLM Zoomcamp!

Together with Evgeniya, Kacper, and our friends at @qdrant_engine, we’ve updated and expanded the Vector Search module, and it’s now live!

Here’s what you’ll explore:

This module covers:

🔸 Getting started with vector databases using Qdrant
🔸 Embedding text data
🔸 Indexing and searching
🔸 RAG with vector search
🔸 Hybrid search techniques

🔥 We’ve also added brand-new hands-on notebooks!

Proud of this collaboration with Qdrant, one of the best open-source vector databases, and excited to help you bring vector search into your real-world RAG applications.

👉 Check out the module: https://github.com/DataTalksClub/llm-zoomcamp/tree/main/02-vector-search
